The abstrakt program is a theoretical model that can serve as a mathematical description for a programming language. Developing an abstract program requires defining the syntax and semantic rules that explicitly outline the structure and meaning of programs. This formalization enables rigorous mathematical analysis and proof techniques to be applied to programming concepts, essentially translating coding challenges into mathematical proofs. This document presents an abstract model for a programming language based on code and specifies evaluation rules that clearly illustrate how program values are determined. Additionally, it establishes a representation theorem that substantiates the soundness of this model and confirms the effectiveness of our abstract representation in modeling the underlying programming language. This achievement offers a framework for investigating key concepts within the programming language, as exemplified by our analysis of the concept of type in the appendix. This abstract model, along with the associated formalization, can be accessed through the Coq proof assistant on the CoqHub platform: <https://coqhub.org/abstract-code/>. Using data from the CANDELS survey, our analysis of nearly 3500 galaxies at a redshift of 1.5 probes the link between a galaxy's mass, shape, and surrounding halo mass. By measuring galaxy size with an established technique and predicting halo mass using stellar masses and concentrations, our model allows us to track this relationship over time. This approach reveals that, at a redshift of 1.5, more massive galaxies tend to have both larger diameters and more extensive halos. As galaxies evolve, this relationship changes: those with higher mass tend to experience more rapid size reduction and less extensive halo expansion. Our findings are consistent with the idea that less massive galaxies are surrounded by smaller halos because their internal matter is quickly absorbed by invaders, while more massive galaxies have greater environmental influence due to their larger halos. This interpretation is supported by the observed trend of more massive galaxies having more saturated halo masses. Our analysis also suggests that the process governing galaxy size is complex and influenced by various factors, including those related to mass, shape, and environmental settings. By studying these dynamics over extended periods of time, our understanding of galaxy assembly and its connection to the surrounding cosmic web becomes clearer. This research provides valuable insights for future research using the James Webb Space Telescope. Furthermore, our data, along with other observational and simulated data sources, reveal potential discrepancies with predictions from ABSPIMS simulations, suggesting a need for additional theoretical explanations. Due to its unique properties, photometry has emerged as a reliable method for estimating aerosol concentrations in the atmosphere. Our research provides an overview of the most recent developments in this field, focusing on the analytical approach that incorporates the effects of aerosols on optical intensity and phase shift in multiple frequencies. This is essential because the optical principle is sensitive to changes in the atmosphere, making it an excellent tool for monitoring aerosol concentrations. Our approach is grounded in the underlying optical system's mathematical description. Recent studies have explored the capabilities of various optical systems, including the use of closed and open loops, as well as phase shift measurements across multiple frequencies, to differentiate between fine and coarse aerosols. By developing a sophisticated mathematical framework, we are better equipped to tackle the complexities of diverse atmospheric conditions and improve the accuracy of aerosol estimations. Ultimately, this will enable the development of practical methods for aerosol assessments, contributing to a broader range of atmospheric research and applications. Specifically, we examined the practical implications of using optical intensity and phase shift measurements in single-frequency and multi-frequency systems. By analyzing the phase shift data across different frequencies, we were able to estimate aerosol concentrations and distinguish between different types of aerosols. Our research demonstrates that by combining intensity and phase shift information, we can enhance the accuracy of aerosol estimations and open up new avenues for atmospheric research. Additionally, we propose to integrate our optical technique with existing monitoring systems to expand its capabilities and make aerosol assessments even more accessible and efficient. By doing so, we are contributing to a wider range of applications in various fields, including meteorology, air quality monitoring, and communications, by facilitating a more detailed understanding of the complex interactions between the atmosphere and electromagnetic radiation. Ultimately, this knowledge will enable us to develop more effective strategies for maintaining a stable connection between terrestrial devices and airborne platforms in harsh atmospheric conditions. To summarize, we have outlined the fundamental principles and recent advancements in aerosol assessments using stellar photometry, highlighting its unique features and practical applications that can improve our understanding of aerosols in the atmosphere. Moving forward, we will continue to develop and refine this technique, leveraging its sensitivity to atmospheric changes to enable precise aerosol estimations that will drive innovative research and development in various fields. We conduct a thorough examination into how photoevaporation and magnetic force can impact the structure of protoplanetary disks by analyzing the characteristics of TW Hydrae, a young stellar object with a close-in planet that experiences mass transmission. Using a combination of radio and X-ray observations, we assess whether the disk undergoes photoevaporation or experiences magnetic force stimulation. We create detailed models for both scenarios, taking into account the impact of photoevaporation on the disk's surface layers and the effect of magnetic force on the disk's global structure. Our photoevaporation model incorporates the disk's surface temperature and pressure while applying a thorough search for the disk's mass loss rate. Our magnetic force model utilizes the approach of 'disk breeze,' where the global ionized gas is driven by thermal pressure, and we calculate the electric field that drives the gas away from the disk. We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle structured monotone inclusion problems. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique used in the Chambolle-Pock 'trend' algorithm, DWIFOB offers an alternative solution. We provide conditions and prove that it yields a globally convergent algorithm with an sublinear rate of convergence. Furthermore, we examine two specific applications of DWIFOB by applying it to convex-concave saddle-point problems and quadratic optimization with a prox-regular perspective. The resulting analysis shows that DWIFOB can be viewed as a naturally weighted forward-backward algorithm. In our numerical experiments, DWIFOB outperforms other methods, such as the Chambolle-Pock 'trend' algorithm and the extrapolated forward-backward algorithm, in various test problems. We also explore the implementation of DWIFOB on a NVIDIA Jetson TX2 GPU using CUDA. The associated code is provided for evaluation purposes. In particular, we examine the performance of DWIFOB when applied to a specific quadratic optimization problem with a prox-regular perspective on a GPU. The time it takes to execute this test on a NVIDIA Jetson TX2 GPU is significantly lower than on a Intel Core i7 CPU. We then examine the performance of DWIFOB by scaling up the test problem and comparing its speed to the Intel Core i7 CPU with the Intel Core i7 TGL CPU. The results show that DWIFOB achieves a notable speedup on the NVIDIA Jetson TX2 GPU. The research demonstrates that DWIFOB offers an efficient and reliable solution to structured monotone inclusion problems, especially when implemented on a GPU. Consequently, it has the potential to facilitate rapid convergence in various applications, including deep learning and signal processing. More broadly, it can empower researchers and engineers to leverage the capabilities of GPUs to analyze and visualize data more effectively. The potential impact is substantial, given the widespread adoption of GPUs in recent years. Therefore, we can expect DWIFOB to make a significant contribution to the field, particularly when applied to monotone inclusion problems involving large-scale data sets. Furthermore, the success of DWIFOB using CUDA on a NVIDIA Jetson TX2 GPU sets the stage for future research to explore the use of deep learning techniques from an optimization perspective. It also presents opportunities for integrating other methods, such as the extrapolated forward-backward algorithm and the Chambolle-Pock 'trend' algorithm, into a unified framework on a GPU. Recent breakthroughs in neural networks have sparked a desire to automate the
design of computer systems, including neural networks themselves. A novel
approach, known as Neural Design Search, seeks to develop more efficient and
effective methods for creating neural networks. This research integrates ideas
from program synthesis, leveraging techniques such as type checking to ensure
quality networks, by translating neural network specifications into code
using the Halide and then generating code through the Synthesis table, thus
connecting NS with formal verification of neural networks. This integration is
the primary contribution of this research, enabling NS to enjoy the benefits of
formal verification for the first time. To accomplish this, the paper introduces
a new framework that extends the concepts of property-directed synthesis and
relaxes the traditional type system, allowing for more flexible network
design. Moreover, the paper presents a novel language that enables precise
specification of neural networks and introduces a new verification algorithm,
allowing NS to be verified for the first time. Finally, the paper showcases
practical applications of NS, including the design of neural networks with
specified computational patterns and the reduction of neural networks to achieve
specified performance levels. These results demonstrate the practical
significance of NS and its potential to revolutionize the design of computer
systems. To facilitate replication, the research includes detailed
demonstrations and the synthesis tables used in this study. \looseness -1

In millimeter wave (mmWave) wireless communication, the combination of high data rate and limited bandwidth requires efficient modulation schemes. However, traditional modulation methods may not be suitable for mmWave systems due to power limitations. To address this challenge, this study introduces a novel multi-carrier encoding method that utilizes orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) and pulse position modulation (PPM). To maximize data transmission efficiency, this scheme has been optimized for both single-user and multi-user applications. The analytical findings are then verified through simulations, which highlight the hybrid encoder's superior performance compared to conventional systems. Notably, this encoding method can achieve notable improvements in spectral efficiency, substantial reductions in power consumption, and enhanced system reliability, particularly in complex scenarios like urban environments. Moreover, the results indicate that the hybrid encoder remains an optimal solution even when there are discrepancies in channel conditions among individual user groups. To summarize, this hybrid encoding method provides a reliable solution for reliable and high-speed data transmission in mmWave systems, making it an ideal choice for a variety of wireless applications. Federated Learning, a framework for collaborative machine learning, enables multiple devices to collaborate on model development without sharing sensitive data. The Federated Learning protocol typically employs local models or aggregation of local parameters on a central server. A newer approach, Federated Distillation, overcomes several limitations by allowing the central server to directly learn the global model distribution from participating devices. However, the need for each device to transmit the entire model on each iteration is inefficient, particularly when the model is complex and devices are resource-constrained. To address this issue, we propose a new technique where the central server learns a compact distillation program that can be executed by each device, reducing the required communication bandwidth and efficiently utilizing available resources. Moreover, to enhance model performance under communication constraints, we introduce a novel program that can withstand data distribution biases, allowing the central server to directly learn from participants without requiring the transmission of biased local models. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach successfully minimizes communication expenses while achieving comparable or even superior performance compared to existing models. Name service problems in Named Data Networking (NDN) require special handling of 
hostname management, particularly when mobile devices are involved. To address this, 
a dynamic name service has been proposed that automatically manages hostnames 
and updates them as devices move within a network. However, the services rely on 
location information that can be inaccurate, over their update rates, or affected 
by network conditions like congestion. This leads to suboptimal performance and 
connection delays. A better approach, the Ideal Dynamic Coordination (IDC) 
algorithm, has been developed with faster convergence and more efficient coordination 
between mobile devices. Comparisons with existing solutions have shown that IDC 
outperforms by reducing the time it takes for devices to recognize each other, 
lowering the likelihood of inaccurate hostname information, and decreasing the impact 
of network problems on services. As a result, IDC leads to faster data transfer 
rates and better system response times for ND-based computing networks. Further 
analysis included simulating real-world scenarios using the FlexRAN system as an 
example, demonstrating that IDC can also improve performance in distributed 
computing and virtualized radio access networks. Finally, measurements have been 
taken to gauge the efficiency of IDC in these environments. Overall, IDC has shown 
promising results that validate its potential as a reliable and efficient solution for 
dynamic hostname management in ND-based computing and mobile ND networks. 
Extensive testing has confirmed that IDC can handle a wide range of traffic without 
notable performance degradation, making it suitable for various network applications 
and environments. To summarize, IDC has been designed to address the challenges 
of dynamic hostname management in mobile ND networks by minimizing the time it 
takes for devices to coordinate with each other, maximizing the accuracy of hostname 
information, and mitigating the effects of network problems on system performance.

encouraging results, leading to its potential as a reliable and efficient solution for 
dynamic hostname management in ND-based computing and mobile ND networks.

We examine the spectral properties of the operator corresponding to the equation of long, thin, planar beams that are connected in a star configuration. Specifically, we investigate the stability of these beams when we apply external forces that cause them to vibrate in specific, extended shapes. Our analysis reveals that when we apply forces that cause the beams to vibrate in specific, two-dimensional shapes, the associated quadratic forms are finite and positive. Conversely, when the beams are forced to vibrate in directions orthogonal to these planes, the associated forms are infinite. Notably, we demonstrate that the stability of these beams is linked to the geometric arrangement of the supports, and provide a straightforward criterion for determining the spectral stability based on this configuration. Moreover, we show that the absence of extended configurational instability is equivalent to the satisfaction of a certain condition in the context of non-local boundary stability. Finally, we illustrate our findings with a concrete example.

We examine the vulnerability of policy learning in reinforcement learning under adversarial conditions and propose a novel attack method that can be executed without access to the model. Our attack estimates the temporal difference error and leverages this estimate to determine the most effective action that can disrupt the agent's performance. Our approach is simplified by applying the mini-batch gradient descent technique, enabling it to be applied to complex models. Our attack has been thoroughly tested on various scenarios, including deep Q-networks, and our experimental findings reveal that it yields substantial returns in comparison to existing attack methods while also avoiding the need for an explicit transition model. Specifically, our attack achieved return values of 450% for deep Q-networks in the Space Invaders game and 300% for the Lunar Lander task, outperforming other attack methods. Moreover, our attack demonstrated superior adaptability by being applicable to a range of RL models, including policy gradient methods and actor-critic algorithms. Our proposed attack represents a significant advancement in this domain as it can be easily replicated and has a broad applicability to various RL models, thereby enabling the evaluation of black-box attacks on a wide range of learning agents. Our code has been publicly released for reproducibility purposes. Additionally, our attack has been integrated into the BlackBoxRL framework for ease of use by the RL community. To address the pressing global issue of energy consumption, this work proposes a novel approach for assessing the power usage of Machining Centers (MCs). By quantifying the energy efficiency of these systems, manufacturers can optimize their operations to reduce energy waste and align MC performance with emerging trends in Industry 4.0, such as the use of digital twins and Real-Time Monitoring and Analysis (RTMA). Our framework consists of two main components: a Bayesian evaluation method for estimating MC power consumption and identifying the most efficient operating points. The second part involves a Genetic Algorithm (GA) that seeks to optimize MC configurations to achieve improved power efficiency, effectively driving MC performance towards optimal operating conditions. Our study demonstrates that the integration of these two techniques yields enhanced power performance, surpassing the capabilities of traditional assessment methods. Furthermore, GA-powered assessments enable manufacturers to make informed decisions by providing valuable insights and recommendations for improving MC configurations. By streamlining the assessment process and offering tailored suggestions, companies can accelerate the optimization of their MCs, thereby reducing energy consumption and aligning with the principles of Industry 4.0 without incurring significant upfront investment. The proposed Bayesian estimation method is universally applicable and can be adapted for use with various MC technologies, while the GA-driven optimization technique can be tailored to suit each machine type with a view to optimizing power efficiency. Our combined approach has been validated through experimental testing of a conventional vertical MC, and the findings indicate that our method is characterized by high levels of accuracy, robustness, and reliability, surpassing the performance of traditional assessment methods and yielding better results than those obtained through manual MC optimization. The proposed approach is expected to contribute positively to the reduction of energy consumption and can be employed by manufacturers to introduce Industry 4.0 trends into their operations at a minimal upfront cost. We find that the lightest process must occur within massive stars due to the lack of suitable candidates among pre-solar material.  The production of nitrogen in space via the nuclear reactions involving carbon in massive stars is confirmed, but we find that the so-called "nitrogen deficit" remains unresolved.  The most plausible explanation for the space-abundance of nitrogen is the ejection of material from both Type II and Type I supernovae.  However, the low supernova ejecta abundance of nitrogen from low-mass stars remains an unresolved issue. Predicting the impact of events on social networks before they happen is a difficult task.
To make this prediction, we develop a new method that uses a model learning from graphs, considering the varying lengths of data sets and event timelines when training and evaluating models.
By applying this approach to scenarios such as analyzing online discussions before a US presidential debate or tracking trends on Reddit before the release of a highly anticipated movie, we improve the accuracy of predictions by up to 12.5% compared to current leading methods.
The accuracy of our model is confirmed through experiments using 12 real-world data sets spanning different online platforms and events, revealing a 3.2% average increase in accuracy over existing solutions.

To facilitate the analysis of binarized matrix market models, we introduce a new sampling method that selects sparse, uniformly distributed binary matrix examples with specified row and column sum patterns. We prove that this algorithm can generate matrices with desired properties in a computationally efficient way, particularly for cases with limited row or column sums. We also present experimental results showing that our approach has a faster average case complexity than the established population limit method, specifically for the Plackett-Burman design and models with out-degree skewed distributions. Additionally, our method is complemented by a online extension that allows for dynamic example generation and two variant implementations that can achieve even better efficiency at the expense of slightly reduced flexibility in example distribution. The proposed sampling method is further exemplified through its application in three empirical case studies, where it is utilized to create binary market models from real-world data and the generated examples are utilized to approach learning problems under specific constraints. Our investigation focuses on binary weight neural networks and demonstrates that quantization increases the network's capacity by altering the kernel realization within a specific functional space. The kernel's continuity dictates its expressiveness; consequently, the network's capacity is influenced by its Lipschitz constant, defined as the kernel's Norma Weighted Matrix (NTK). During quantization, the binary weight vector collapses, resulting in an approximate kernel realization that leads to an enlarged training data set and, consequently, enhanced generalization performance. Our analysis provides a quantitative framework that relates quantization bits to the network's generalization capabilities. Moreover, our findings suggest that the benefits of quantization can be harnessed even in fully connected binary neural networks, thereby extending the scope of previous research. Additionally, our study offers a practical approach to selecting the optimal quantization bit depth and achieves comparable or superior outcomes compared to the traditional full-precision setting. The proposed methodology is versatile and can be applied to various quantized neural network architectures, such as those employing skip connections in residual networks. Our theoretical conclusions are substantiated by numerical experiments that demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, particularly when combined with regularization techniques. Furthermore, our research facilitates the development of bit-depth optimization strategies that prioritize generalization over efficiency while still accommodating resource constraints. Consequently, our work bridges the gap between theoretical and practical knowledge of quantized neural networks, thereby providing actionable insights for practitioners. Accurately predicting when two or more interconnected time series become synchronized is a crucial task in various scientific contexts, including climate modeling and cardiovascular research. In finance, the idea of synchronization has been explored in the context of asset price movements and macroeconomic indicators. Our research focuses on developing a novel approach for predicting synchronization by analyzing financial time series. We applied the cross-recurrence framework to forecast synchronization in two pairs of time series: the S&P 500 stock index and the VIX volatility index. The results of our experiments demonstrated that, compared to random predictions, our approach successfully forecasted synchronization with a high degree of accuracy, reaching up to 85% for one of the tested pairs, and showed significant statistical significance. Furthermore, we uncovered a significant and positive correlation between forecasted synchronization periods and future stock market returns, indicating that our method has the potential to yield valuable trading strategies. We also compared our approach with an alternative method involving autocorrelation analysis and found that it outperformed the latter in all tested aspects. Therefore, our study highlights the effectiveness of the cross-recurrence framework in forecasting synchronization and extracting valuable information from it. Additionally, our findings have practical implications for developers of trading systems that utilize synchronization-based rules. Enhancing click-through rate (CTR) is a critical goal for advertisers that can be achieved by optimizing the visibility of their ads. To accomplish this, advertisers allocate budgets to ads that are expected to generate the most clicks. Current forecasting methods, however, primarily rely on historical ad performance and do not consider the potential impact of viewer preferences on CTR. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel ad forecasting approach called Enhance CTR (E-CTR), which takes into account both the visual content of ads and viewer preferences. By leveraging a neural network to analyze ad images and predict viewer preferences, we can select ads that are more likely to appeal to a target audience. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of E-CTR in surpassing traditional forecasting methods by up to 26.8%. Additionally, our approach enables more precise ad allocation, resulting in a 10.5% to 20.6% increase in overall CTR. Our findings can be applied to improve ad forecasting and enhance CTR through the analysis of visual ad content and viewer preferences. The associated code for this project is available at https://github.com/chenyong1019/E-CTR. The dataset used in this study can be accessed via HTTPS://github.com/chenyong1019/Visual_Ads_dataset. Our experiments involved collecting data from two e-commerce platforms, which yielded a dataset consisting of 1,440 ads, 2,560 images, and 3,020 user preferences. Our approach was then compared to traditional forecasting methods, with the results presented in Figure 1. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of our findings, we employed k-fold cross-validation. Notably, our approach outperformed the control methods in all scenarios (see Figure 2). Our analysis also revealed that the visual content of ads plays a significant role in CTR forecasting. To facilitate the reproduction of our results, we have made our code and dataset available for download. Our study contributes to the body of work on ad forecasting and enhances CTR by leveraging the analysis of visual ad content and viewer preferences. Ultimately, our approach can be applied by advertisers to optimize their ad allocation and maximize their return on investment. To forecast wildfire aerosols' spread, researchers have turned to machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques, but they struggle to adapt to new regions without extensive training data. In response, researchers are developing physics-informed deep learning models that incorporate physical principles and are adaptable to various geographic areas with minimal data requirements. In this study, a novel deep learning approach is proposed that uses filter-based air quality measurements and aerosols' radiance data to forecast their spread across a given region. To test its effectiveness, this method was applied to the western provinces of Canada, utilizing three satellite remote-sensing data streams and comparing its performance to a traditional DL model. Results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms the comparison model, delivering more accurate forecasts and reducing the need for extensive training data. With its flexibility and efficiency, this method has the potential to aid air quality forecasting and decision-making in various applications, including smoke aerosols' forecasting for wildfire-prone areas. Theoretical models in location privacy analysis assume a uniform prior distribution over possible locations, which does not accurately reflect real-life situations where individuals often return to specific locations, like their homes. To address this, a new location privacy framework is introduced that takes into account non-uniform prior distributions. A specific method, the Weibull distribution, is then applied to develop an optimal strategy for an attacker seeking to determine an user's location within a one-dimensional space. An approach based on the dynamic programming technique provides a solution, further enhanced by presenting a simplified version, along with determining when the optimal strategy can be simplified as finding the minimum variance of the posterior probability function. Additionally, a location tracking privacy protocol is proposed that integrates the new framework with a well-established tracking scheme, demonstrating an improvement in privacy for specific cases. Finally, a comparison between this new framework and previous methods, including using the Kullback-Leibler divergence, is performed to validate the introduced framework's effectiveness. We found a clear pattern and used this information to improve accuracy when predicting site of origin based on brain connectivity patterns. By considering the limitations of each site's measurements, we developed a new approach that uses Bayesian statistics to classify the data, and this method performed better than previous techniques, especially in cases where data is limited. Our results will likely contribute to future multisite research in brain function. Fisher's mean effect has been debated over its importance in meta-analysis. However, its causal significance is not well understood. We resolve this ambiguity by demonstrating that the mean effect is a form of weighted arithmetic mean, and thus, a causal quantity when the weights and effects are both causal. Furthermore, when these conditions are not met, the mean effect is a pseudomean value. We provide the criteria to determine causality for both weights and effects, highlighting the importance of Fisher's mean effect in meta-analysis. We also introduce a novel parameter, the causality index, to assess the essential condition of Fisher's mean effect being a causal quantity. Based on our analysis, the causality index can be utilized to investigate the significance of Fisher's mean effect in both individual studies and overall meta-analyses. We also find that the inclusion or exclusion of null studies does not affect the causality index, and thus, they do not alter the outcome of a meta-analysis. We validate our findings through simulations, and illustrate our approach with a practical example involving two meta-analyses related to the efficacy of the COVID-19 vaccine. Our results provide a clear understanding of the causal importance of Fisher's mean effect in meta-analysis, and show that including or excluding null studies does not impact its outcome. We conclude that the mean effect should only be employed when both weights and effects are causal, and recommend the use of alternative measures, such as the pseudomean value, when this condition is not met. We also propose that the pseudomean and causality approaches should be reported in conjunction with each other in future meta-analyses. Furthermore, our results can be easily replicated by generating the necessary R code, and illustrate the long-standing debate on the significance of Fisher's mean effect having finally been put to rest. Future large-scale robotic missions to other planets could benefit significantly from using local materials to fuel their activities, however, these robots need to be able to move around efficiently while carrying the weight of the propellant. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a novel approach that uses legged locomotion to take advantage of propulsion generated by expelling propellant out of the back, much like the movement of some aquatic creatures. By utilizing the expelling force, the robot can achieve higher efficiency and increase its stability through dynamic balance. This paper presents a new concept for bipedal robots that integrates propulsion and balance systems, and we've supported this idea with simulations in three distinct environments: vacuum, air with minimal resistance, and air with significant resistance, performing tasks such as walking and propulsive maneuvers. The results show that the dynamic movement and balance capabilities of the robot increase its stability and allow it to achieve higher efficiency when compared to traditional propulsion methods. Moreover, when moving through air with resistance, the average speed increased by more than 30% when compared to static propulsion. The research presented here provides a foundation for future work, and we believe that the concepts presented can be applied to various configurations of robotic systems. Additionally, we've explored the relationship between the shape of the propellant container and its effect on the dynamic movement and balance capabilities of the robot. The most efficient dynamic movement and balance capabilities were achieved using a container shape that produces a force that pushes the robot forward as propellant is expelled, resulting in increased stability and a higher speed when moving through air with resistance. The research presented here was done using three-dimensional simulations in Genomic Simulation, an open-source tool for high-throughput simulations, and we provide a detailed guide on how to apply the research to actual hardware using the examples of a bipedal robot designed for exploration of other planets and a quadcopter. We've run the most extensive simulations yet of the initial moments following the merger of a compact binary consisting of a black hole and a neutron star. Our findings cover the first two seconds of the merger. The simulation accounted for the effects of radiation, magnetic fields, and irregularities in the neutron star's internal structure. The outcome was consistently a black hole surrounded by a massive disk of accretion, accompanied by powerful jets of matter. The behavior of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in the disk varied based on the initial strength and configuration of magnetic fields. In scenarios with weaker magnetic fields (initial magnetic flux density below 10^14 G), the disk displayed stable, long-wavel lengths, whereas with stronger magnetic fields (above 10^14) G, the disk became turbulent with short wavelengths. The initial magnetic field configuration significantly influenced the resulting accretion rates, with axisymmetric fields producing lower accretion rates than fields aligned radially. The simulated accretion rates matched those of previous analyses, albeit with higher rates in this study. The merger's energy output was consistent across various simulations, amounting to 2.1% of the initial neutron star's mass-energy equivalent. The outcome of our research is largely independent of the initial neutron star's internal structure. The simulations indicate that the neutron star survives the merger, retaining up to 95% of its initial mass. The final black hole and neutron star masses were found to conform to general relativity, with the neutron star experiencing significant radial contraction and heating due to the emission and transfer of energy. The rotation period of the black hole and neutron star was found to be consistently around three milliseconds. The accretion by the black hole was found to be consistent with the standard thin-disk model, with the accretion rates matched in various simulations. The disk's mass was found to be consistently around 0.049 solar mass, with the majority of the neutron star's initial mass being either accreted by the black hole or stored in the disk and jets. The initial moments following the merger saw a massive energy output, with the majority of the energy being carried by jets and a smaller portion by the disk's radiation. This paper delves into the behavior of a system that starts with an elevated level of noise compared to its typical counterpart, specifically in regards to quadratic convergence towards a quasi-stationary equilibrium known as a Q-process. We examine two primary scenarios: one where the system's parameters gradually shift over time and another where the anomaly in noise levels is temporary, leading to a sudden transition, both of which exhibit consistent convergence towards a Q-process. Our analysis spans three main methods: obtaining quantitative estimates for the first scenario, exploring the dynamics of a two-state system, and demonstrating a lack of convergence towards a Q-process under specific conditions. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the anomalies that can occur in equilibrium behavior and highlights their dependence on the dynamics of the underlying system. We also discuss the implications of these results for various scientific applications, including population dynamics and chemical reactions. Furthermore, our work contributes to the development of a new theoretical framework known as quasi-stationary equilibrium theory, which enables the examination of systems that exist in an unusual equilibrium state. We derive explicit estimates for both the time and level of anomaly in noise levels that can occur in systems where the rate of change in population dynamics is constant, as well as systems where the rate of change is time-dependent. We also find that the level of anomaly in noise levels increases as the anomaly's duration decreases, except in cases where the rate of change in population dynamics is constant, which instead leads to a leveling off of this anomaly. A multi-agent collaborative approach is applied to an original zero-sum matrix game to evaluate the extent to which robots can effectively coordinate with one another despite limitations in computation and communication capabilities. A dual approach combined with a standard dual-iteration algorithm is utilized to derive optimal strategies for each agent. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this approach enables efficient coordination between robots, particularly when bandwidth is limited. Additionally, we analyze the impact of communication constraints on the outcome, revealing that increased restrictions may lead to decreased performance. Notably, we observe that even basic robotic systems can achieve superior outcomes through collaboration. A real-world experiment involving small robotic systems validates the findings of the simulation, showcasing the potential for improved outcomes and reduced movement requirements when robots work together. Research into the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) has been conducted through the analysis of charged particle collisions, particularly in lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). A specific observable, $\Delta \eta \rho_{\text{az}}$, has been used to investigate the influence of the CME, although it is also susceptible to other effects such as global momentum conservation. To isolate the CME influence, the dependence of $\Delta \eta \rho_{\text{az}}$ on centrality was examined and found to be proportional to the charged-particle density. To further understand the CME, the CME influence was suppressed by examining forward-and-backward and co- and counter- flowing correlations in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The results indicate that the CME influence is significantly limited, particularly in the 5.02 TeV collisions, which can be attributed to the reduced influence of global momentum conservation. The findings suggest that local charge non-conservation may also limit the CME influence, and that the CME influence can be quantitatively estimated using a relativistic hydrodynamics model. Therefore, these studies contribute to a deeper understanding of the CME and provide a means of accurately detecting it in heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, the data collected can be used to determine the transport coefficients of quark-gluon plasma. The data presented represent the most comprehensive investigation of the CME influence to date and offer insights into the spatial and temporal characteristics of the CME. The data also provide a framework for further analysis, such as studying the CME in collisions of smaller systems and at lower energies. The ultimate goal of these studies is to detect the CME at the LHC's lower energy setting, as well as at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). The research also paves the way for future investigations at the Future Circular Collider (FCC). Previous studies focused on specific platforms such as Kickstarter or Indiegogo but did not compare the common crowd indicators across multiple platforms. To address this, this study analyzed successful projects from both Kickstarter and Indiegogo to determine the shared and distinct indicators that contribute to a project's fundraising success. The analysis considered both project and creator characteristics as well as crowd interactions. The results revealed that, although there are some platform-specific variables, the crowd's response plays a crucial role in a project's success, regardless of the platform. In industrial settings, where efficiency is a top priority, optimizing the sequence of tasks for multi-point robotic manipulators can significantly reduce production time and costs. To tackle this challenge, a novel approach called Sequential Manipulator Sequencing (SMS) has been developed, allowing for simultaneous scheduling of multiple manipulators' task sequences. SMS effectively minimizes the total time required to complete all tasks, demonstrating better results than traditional methods in experimental case studies. Building on SMS, two improved algorithms, SMS-GC1 and SMS-GC2, have been introduced, which leverage task clustering to enhance performance. These algorithms exploit the inherent structure of manipulator interdependencies, applying greedy techniques to optimize results. In comparison to SMS, SMS-GC1 demonstrates better average results, while SMS-GC2 exhibits a higher percentage of optimal solutions. Consequently, SMS-GC1 and SMS-GC2 outperform alternative methods, including those based on constraint programming and local search, as validated by comprehensive experiments involving up to 20 manipulators. Our investigation uncovers a previously unrecognized issue in video search platforms - a preference for diversity in origin that affects the search outcomes. This means that search algorithms can inadvertently favor videos from rare sources over those from more established providers. To highlight and rectify this issue, we have developed a novel auditing technique that focuses on the diversity of video origins in search outcomes. Our technique, which is grounded in both theoretical and practical knowledge, uses a virtual agent to manipulate a video search platform and measure its source diversity bias. Employing our auditing technique on YouTube and Vimeo, two prominent video hosting platforms with different levels of diversity in video origins, we conduct extensive experiments that demonstrate the presence of a source diversity bias in YouTube but not in Vimeo. Furthermore, our experiments show that adjusting the diversity of video origins in YouTube can affect the ranking of search outcomes. This finding underscores the importance of using objective measures like source diversity bias in conjunction with other evaluation metrics in video search and retrieval. Our work also identifies potential avenues for improving the diversity bias of video search platforms and suggests future research directions. In wireless communication systems, interference not only lessens the quality of the desired signal but also the system's overall capacity due to limited transmission rates. This research targets improving wireless networks' efficiency by increasing throughput, beyond what's possible with traditional maximum ratio combining techniques. To achieve this, we present a novel approach based on a probabilistic transmission strategy called "probability shaping," which aims to maximize interference-robustness in wireless networks. By modeling each user's data as a binary process with a specific probability of one and zero, we seek to find the optimal transmission probabilities to ensure reliable data transfer while minimizing the impact of interference. This is framed as an optimization problem, with solutions provided for special cases, including two-user and multi-user networks. Simulation results demonstrate the potential for significant gains in wireless networks using probability-shaped transmission. Specifically, for a two-user network with identical channel conditions and strong interference, the proposed strategy can increase throughput by up to 300%, even if the network operator attempts to keep interference under 10 dB. Furthermore, for more complex networks with varying channel conditions, the strategy can yield improvements of up to 500%. These gains are attributed to the ability of probability-shaped transmission to adapt to the unique characteristics of each user's data and the interference affecting the wireless network. By applying probability shaping, wireless networks can move beyond traditional capacity limits, even in the presence of interference. This research provides a framework for optimizing these probabilities and highlights the potential benefits of probability-shaped transmission in wireless networks. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in node classification, they are hampered by a need for extensive labeled data, a costly resource. To mitigate this issue, we focus on enhancing pseudo-labeling, a semi-supervised technique that generates high-quality labels for unsupervised nodes using trained model predictions from labeled nodes. Our proposed GNN-Pseudo approach incorporates an unsupervised self-training module, which includes an innovative forward and backward graph refinement process. This process combines node features with pseudo-labels, yielding improved accuracy and convergence speed in graph classification tasks. Our experiments on six datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, revealing a 4-10% boost in accuracy over standard semi-supervised GNNs and a 10-20% improvement over existing pseudo-labeling methods. Our findings indicate that GNN-Pseudo can efficiently utilize limited labels and unsupervised nodes to achieve notable performance gains. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyu-1995/Graph-Pseudo.

In video analysis tasks, the alignment of frames is frequently required to enable systems to understand video content across different time points. Current feature-based frame alignment methods are suitable for various video analysis tasks but have several drawbacks, including high computational cost, fragility to outliers, and difficulty in being scaled up for processing multiple videos. To address these issues, a new method called PatchNet has been developed, which uses a network to efficiently match video content between frames. PatchNet employs a patch-matching approach to align small video segments, leveraging a robust encoder to convert each into a distinctive code. This code is then used to measure the similarity between frame segments, while the network's parameters are optimized through a regression-based loss function that can identify outliers and be fine-tuned for specific tasks. Notably, PatchNet is scalable and suitable for analyzing multiple videos, as well as being used in various video analysis tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of PatchNet, which outperforms existing methods in several tasks while significantly reducing the processing time by an order of magnitude. For example, it takes only 0.13 seconds to analyze a 10,000 frame video, which is an impressive 50 times faster than the second best method. Additionally, PatchNet is versatile and can be used in various video analysis tasks, such as action recognition, video classification, and vehicle tracking. Overall, PatchNet offers an efficient and scalable solution for video analysis tasks that rely on frame alignment. To validate the method and demonstrate its capabilities, the developers of PatchNet have created the VOS-MVS Dataset, which contains 2,000 videos with rich annotations. Furthermore, the dataset and related code have been made publicly available, allowing researchers to access the VOS-MVS resources. To evaluate the generalization of PatchNet, the researchers applied the method to multiple video datasets and compared its performance with other state-of-the-art models. Notably, PatchNet consistently performs well across various video datasets, which demonstrates its versatility and generalization capabilities. To confirm the feasibility of PatchNet in real-world applications, the researchers analyzed the processing time of the method when applied to multiple videos. We examine a one-dimensional asymptotically stationary, TASEP system with multiple exit points and periodic time intervals. Our research focuses on how to distribute a multi-point system's initial data across these periods in a way that ensures stationary behavior at all times. We introduce the concept of a blockage sequence, which represents the amount of a particular type of blockage occurring in a specific time interval, and establish its uniqueness and importance in achieving stationary states. It is discovered that for a system with t periods and e exits, the blockage sequence is represented by a vector of length e, and the possible values for each element of this sequence are limited to the range [0,1). We devise an iterative method for allocating a system's initial data, and demonstrate that our approach leads to a stationary state characterized by a specific distribution of the blockage sequence. Our results are verified through numerical simulations, and the associated proof involves solving a system of equations known as the ASEP-Q matrix problem. It is further found that the desired blockage sequence can be obtained by taking a convex combination of the perfect blocking and non-blocking states, and the weights of this combination are determined by solving another system of equations. Our research provides a solution to the problem of multi-point allocation in discrete-time TASEP, and offers insights into how to achieve stationary states in systems with exit points and periodic time intervals. Moreover, our results give a detailed description of the time-dependent evolution of a multi-point system, which is useful in various applications. Our research can be applied in a wide range of scenarios, such as traffic management and cell biology, where a system's behavior needs to be optimized or a particular state needs to be achieved. It is notable that our approach allows for a detailed analysis of a system's microstructure, and how it evolves over time. Our research offers a flexible framework that can be adapted to address a range of allocation problems in a comprehensive and general manner. Our results are precise and offer a detailed description of how to achieve a desired state, which is beneficial for making a priori predictions about a system's behavior. Our research provides a theoretical foundation that can be used to develop algorithms and models for a wide range of applications. As a result, new zero(s) of the product function $f(z) + \lambda g(z)$ emerge, describing a diverse range of behaviors. Specifically, our analysis covers situations where these additional zeros are isolated, form a cluster, or encircle the original zero. Additionally, our findings have implications in the fields of statistical physics, specifically in the context of the two-phase transition, where the behaviors of the involved polynomials can be linked to the presence or absence of complex zeros. Moreover, our analysis is crucial in understanding the behavior of the Taylor series of the function $f(z) + \lambda g(z)$ when $\lambda$ is very small or very large, which is essential in both statistical physics and complex analysis. Lastly, our investigation is crucial in determining the leading asymptotic behavior of the curve of a complex polynomial's non-zero zeros. The $W^{\pm}Z$ production process in particle-particle collisions offers a critical opportunity to examine the polarization properties of gauge bosons, which can aid in understanding the fundamental theory known as the Standard Model and potential new physics phenomena.  Researchers have successfully detected $W^{\pm}Z$ events resulting from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, captured by the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, an experiment that operates at or near this energy.  Utilizing 139/fb of accumulated data, $W^{\pm}Z$ production events were analyzed to establish limits on the joint polarization states of gauge bosons.  By analyzing the angular distributions of leptons produced by $W^{\pm}$ and $Z$ decays, evidence of joint polarization states was found at a 4.3 standard deviation confidence level, consistent with expectations.  Additionally, upper limits on the joint polarization states were determined to be less than 0.04 and 0.06 in any given direction.  These findings mark the first detection of gauge boson joint polarization states in $W^{\pm}Z$ production and the most stringent limits on polarization states to date.  These results have been translated into constraints on the model of electroweak interactions, specifically the Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix, with implications for the mass of the W boson and Higgs boson when paired with experimental results from electroweak precision measurements.  These findings serve as the most stringent constraints on the joint polarization states of gauge bosons in $W^{\pm}Z$ production and the joint angular distribution of leptons, offering a new standard in experimental research.  These results have also led to the establishment of a new analysis technique, the differential distribution of cross-sections, with the potential to expand our understanding of particle physics.  Finally, these results have provided evidence of the effectiveness of the ATLAS experiment at detecting complex phenomena through the examination of particle distributions.  This research has further solidified the role of the ATLAS experiment as a leading detector in the study of particle physics at the Large Hadron Collider. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a large-scale linear system, speeding up convergence can significantly impact the overall IPM efficiency. This is typically achieved by utilizing generalized minimum residual (GMRES)-type Krylov solvers. However, fully utilizing interior point method capabilities requires precise control over when to terminate the iterative process. While residual norms may indicate sufficient convergence for many applications, they do not guarantee an optimal solution, particularly when dealing with noisy data or when working with solvers like full orthogonalization storage (FOM) that do not naturally provide termination criteria.

To address this challenge, we introduce an iterative termination criterion that leverages an orthogonal polynomial of degree $m$ to project the residual onto the subspace spanned by the matrix-vector products $v_j=A^Ty_j$. This projection, combined with a threshold and the Euclidean norm, enables us to terminate the iterative process more effectively. To make this criterion applicable to any Krylov solver, we derive a corresponding expression for the preconditioned case and streamline the computational burden by reducing it to a single vector calculation.

We have assessed the machine semantics of proto-Quipper-M, a hybrid high-level quantum circuit description language, using two established mathematical frameworks. First, we established the relationship between quantum circuits and unitary operators through a formal continuation process. Additionally, we defined a formal semantics for proto-Quipper-M by applying a structural compilation approach that transforms the description into a suitable quantum circuit notation. Our investigation demonstrates the equivalence between the machine semantics and the standard quantum circuit description, thereby providing a formal basis for analyzing the semantics of proto-Quipper-M and related similar description languages. Furthermore, this analysis enables us to employ formal methods to prove that these description languages preserve the essential properties of quantum circuits, such as unitarity and the solvability of certain computational tasks. These outcomes will likely have a positive impact on the broader research community by facilitating the effective interaction of quantum engineers and theoretical quantum computing experts. The material presented in this paper will serve as a foundation for a future formal proof of the type-S and correctness criteria in Quipper-M, as well as an extension to higher-order description languages. Moreover, this work may be applied to other quantum circuit description languages by incorporating the described frameworks. The full details of our investigation can be accessed at arXiv:2101.00024 and 2101.00023. This critical point occurs when the matrix size reaches a threshold where the average gap between eigenvalues or eigenvalues and the boundary first appears. Our scaling analysis reveals a crossover from a power-law behavior in larger matrices to a Gaussian distribution, and we establish two critical exponents that characterize this transition. By analyzing the number of singular states in mesoscopic systems, we further demonstrate that our scaling approach is valid and allows us to identify a critical point and associated exponent governing the transition to singular states. Our methodology is general and can be applied to other statistical models to uncover the underlying mechanics of critical phenomena. Additionally, the onset of critical phenomena in magnetic or thermal two-point correlations in mesoscopic systems was investigated, and a new scaling law was developed, which enabled the determination of critical exponents and provided a comprehensive description of the behavior near the critical point. We introduce a novel approach to improve structured text recognition by incorporating a preference model for regular expressions. This preference model, already effective in text editing and code completion, enhances the accuracy of specific line patterns in structured text, such as addresses and dates. However, it demands significant training data, typically not available for recognition tasks. To overcome this limitation, our preference model is designed with a modular structure, allowing it to be solely trained on lines that conform to regular expressions, thus being transferable to various structured text recognition tasks. Our technique exhibits exceptional results on texts with line-based patterns like addresses and invoices, and can be combined with other models for maximum accuracy. The source code for our approach is available at https://github.com/mikep/regexp-favoring-CER. The fundamental concept of web visibility suggests that any webpage with a suitable enough content of specific length can be discovered by a generic query from a search engine like Google. However, our research demonstrates that Google's personalized search results in reality limit the discoverability to around 4 out of 10 relevant webpages. This study employs a novel method of systematic querying, contrasting with the typical human information-seeking behavior, to assess discoverability. Two controlled experiments were conducted, involving a total of 1,179 queries and 34,970 webpages, to evaluate the extent of discoverability and its dependence on webpage characteristics, such as age, and the level of correspondence between query terms and webpage content. Our results show that webpages with query-related information in their titles are 1.3 times more likely to be discovered, while older webpages have a 0.06% higher discoverability rate compared to newer ones. This research provides the first empirical evidence of the impact of personalized web search results on discoverability and highlights the significant underestimation of relevant webpages that may go undiscovered due to Google's personalized search. Two technical advances are introduced - the evaluation of ranking distributions and correspondence analysis - which can aid in understanding and interpreting the results of studies on web discovery and may be applied to other fields as well. Finally, this research raises important implications and potential consequences of relying solely on generic web searches for various purposes, including information retrieval, research, and commercial activities. Automatically creating programs from visual specifications is a challenging task.
Recent research has made progress in this area through graph synthesis, which translates
visual elements into a graph representation to be generated as code. A critical aspect
of this process is graph identification, where specific visual components are mapped
to graph nodes to facilitate the synthesis process. While traditional machine learning
approaches struggle with graph identification due to their fixed representations, a
new Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture has been developed to learn and
generalize graph identification. This model leverages flow diagrams to learn the
correspondence between program flow control and graph structures, enabling graph
identification. Through evaluation on two datasets, the proposed CNN architecture
outperformed existing methods, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability. 
Notably, this approach excels on datasets with diverse program flow control patterns. 
To further validate its performance, a detailed study was conducted, involving
graph identification and synthesis training with human-programmed graphs and subsequent
testing on graphs generated by a graph randomizer. The CNN model achieved a 100%
identification rate on these test graphs, showcasing its capability to learn and
generalize graph identification. The findings highlight the potential of this CNN
architecture as a versatile tool for graph identification in graph synthesis. 
Furthermore, its success suggests that graph synthesis can be applied to a broader
range of domains, including graph identification. 
To facilitate further research, the proposed CNN architecture and accompanying
code have been made available publically. 
In addition, an analysis of the underlying graph structures of program flow control
was conducted, yielding key insights that may inform future research. 
To verify the efficacy of the proposed CNN architecture, a comparison study was
performed, involving evaluations on four distinct graph synthesis datasets. 
The outcomes revealed that the CNN architecture yielded superior results, with
considerably shorter training times, thereby establishing its superiority. 
Consequently, the CNN architecture is now recommended as the preferred approach
for graph synthesis tasks.

experiments were performed, involving evaluations on three distinct graph synthesis
datasets.

particularly impressive performance on a dataset featuring program flow control. 
A closer examination of the dataset revealed that the images contained a mix of
structural and line features.

To overcome this issue, researchers have developed diminution techniques, essentially methods to substantially reduce model complexity while preserving its essential features. This study focuses on diminiton techniques in climate research, specifically analyzing models derived from differential equations and proto-type models of atmospheric and oceanic circulation. A key aspect is the evaluation of these methods against their intended purpose: identifying the parameters that have the greatest impact on the model outcomes. By incorporating concepts from perturbation theory and multiple scale methods, researchers can identify the most relevant factors, ultimately leading to a more efficient use of computational resources. A crucial outcome is the development of simplified mathematical models that can be solved exactly, providing valuable insights into the complex climate systems. This, in turn, may lead to the design of more targeted numerical models and improved analytical tools for climate research. To facilitate accurate dosage delivery during colonoscopies, it's crucial to precisely track the gastrointestinal (GI) tract's location and movement. Leveraging positron emission tomography (PET) imaging in conjunction with an affordable, wearable radio-isotope badge, our research outlines a novel approach for automatic GI canal segmentation in dynamic PET images. This approach involves no alterations to the PET imaging protocol, as the focus solely resides on the analysis of the PET images. To address the sequence variability inherent in dynamic PET images, our proposed solution employs a two-and-a-half-dimensional convolutional neural network (2.5D CNN). The integration of temporal information and the consideration of adjacent PET images enable the segmentation process to encompass both temporal and transverse aspects, with the capability to start segmentation only after the canal is partially detected in an initial image. The performance of our method was demonstrated on a colonoscopy simulation, where it successfully identified the GI canal in 94% of the frames, following an initial detection in 88% of the sequences. Our research provides a cost-effective and accurate solution for automatic GI canal segmentation, which can be further adapted for various clinical applications. Our categorization is built upon the concept of central elements, which divide the algebras into distinct classes. Developing an automated system to generate engaging stories about time-series data from various domains has remained a complex challenge in the field of natural language generation. Existing neural story generation models often rely on domain-specific knowledge, which can result in stories tailored to a single domain, or else produce generic yet unengaging stories lacking essential details. To overcome this limitation, we propose TCube, a novel neural story generation model that extracts key events from a series of time-stamped data and crafts a narrative around these events across multiple domains, including finance and sports. TCube employs a unique combination of a event extractor and two sequence generators to produce coherent and engaging stories. Our experiments demonstrate that TCube surpasses state-of-the-art neural story generation models in both the finance and sports domains in terms of both story coherence and engagingness. Moreover, we demonstrate through analysis that TCube is capable of generating stories that are both more coherent and engaging due to its ability to focus on event-based storytelling. Our findings and model implementations are publicly available at https://www.aisec.ucla.edu/~jiaxun/p/TCube.

The temporal difference mechanism inherent to spiking neural networks has led to the notion that they may be capable of delivering more accurate classification outcomes while consuming less energy compared to conventional neural networks. Nevertheless, the notion that temporal differences confer an energy-saving benefit to SNNs remains unverified, and their potential to outperform their non-blocking counterparts in classification performance remains unverified as well. In an effort to validate these claims, we designed an expanded version of the original temporal difference-based SNN framework by integrating novel, high-performance activation functions along with an efficient spike-propagation technique. We then systematically evaluated our revised model on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets in terms of both classification accuracy and computational efficiency. Our results demonstrate that the original model and our expanded version exhibit comparable performance and energy efficiency. Notably, we discovered that the proposed model achieves a remarkable 47.5% reduction in the number of spikes while maintaining 2% higher accuracy compared to the baseline CNN model on the MNIST dataset. Our findings also reveal that the proposed model exhibits exceptional time-dependent robustness and outperforms other contemporary SNN models in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Our research reveals that, unlike in SCADM, adding more flavors causes the deconfinement transition to transition from first-order to second-order, with the phase transition becoming more complex as the number of flavors increases. This phenomenon can be attributed to the disruption of chiral symmetry, leading to a non-trivial impact on the polaron condensation. In addition, our findings suggest that the mechanism responsible for deconfinement and chiral symmetry breaking differs when the number of flavors is low versus high. Ultimately, our data is consistent with the predictions of two theories: SO(Nf) Lattice Gauge Theory and the 3D Polyakov loop theory for large Nf, with the latter exhibiting a second-order transition in the critical region without a non-trivial fixed point. Our work also provides insight into phase transitions in a broader context of gauge theories. Given the presence of a first-order deconfinement transition in two-flavor SO(6) and SO(8) theories, we propose that a line of first-order phase transitions may exist for theories with even Nc ≤ 10, extending beyond three dimensions. Interpreting complex machine learning models is a crucial task to gain deeper insights into the data. While Attention-based methods can explain the contribution of each feature in a model, they are not universally applicable and can be difficult to use, especially for models like Random Forests and Gradient Boosting. Our proposed method, called Attribution Graph, is an alternative approach that enables feature interpretation in various models by creating a graph linking important features together. Our technique is particularly useful for analyzing decision paths in Tree Ensembles and can be visualized for easier understanding. By analyzing the structure of our Attribution Graph, we can identify important features and subgraphs that indicate model weaknesses or biases. Our method is exemplified through applications in recidivism prediction and medical diagnosis. A demo is available on our website: https://attribution-graph.com. To address this issue, our approach utilizes hardware-supported Trusted Execution Environments to establish a secure federated learning framework, specifically optimized for edge devices such as mobile platforms and laptops. By integrating this technology, users can train models using another device's Trusted Execution Environment, without needing to buy specialized hardware or make complex settings. Our system allows users to train models across different devices, even when they have an incompatible operating system, simply by connecting them via a cable. Through our results, we demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements in training efficiency, particularly when compared to conventional methods. For instance, model training can be completed 3.4 to 4.5 times faster, with reductions in bandwidth usage of up to 13.8 times and increases in convergence speed of up to 2.4 times. These gains are achieved by efficiently compressing model updates, as well as strategically selecting the devices to train on. Our approach has been successfully tested on various scenarios, with a notable example involving a mobile device (Google Pixel 4) training a model using a laptop, while an attacker using the same device to launch a brute force attack on the system was unable to access the data. We introduce a concept called timeloops to automate the system call policies for containerized applications, allowing containers to make authoritative decisions about the system calls permitted to their child processes. Our timeloops approach leverages the capabilities of unikernels and user-level kernel APIs to create a shared framework for developing system call policies, tailored to the needs of individual applications. By separating the system call policy from the underlying execution environment, timeloops facilitate the use of common tools and enable the integration of multiple applications through tunneled network connections. To demonstrate the effectiveness of timeloops, we have implemented a unique network stack and developed a proof-of-concept distributed web service, comprising a main application and multiple components, each running in its own container and accompanied by a timeloop. Our results show that the timeloops-based system call policy is both efficient and secure. Following a brief discussion on the security aspects, we conclude by highlighting the key advantages of the timeloops approach. Our code is freely available online at a GitHub repository. Furthermore, we have created two technical reports, each detailing our research approach, the results obtained so far, and our future plans, a first report dated October 2020 and a second report dated July 2021. Furthermore, we have started collaborating with the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) by submitting a draft proposal for a new Internet standard, "User-level kernel APIs," and have become involved in the standardization process. We have investigated the thermal properties of doped graphene, consisting of multiple graphene flakes connected to multiple leads, under finite-temperature conditions. Our research shows that thermal fluctuations can cause electrostatic interactions between flakes in doped graphene, resulting in a significant increase in the specific heat at low temperatures. This effect is most pronounced when the temperature approaches the interaction strength between flakes. Notably, this behavior is distinct from the thermal expansion of doped single graphene flakes, where the specific heat remains constant at very low temperatures, and instead follows a $T^3$ increase at higher temperatures. Our research also demonstrates that this Shielding Effect can be observed in the specific heat through both average and fluctuating thermal currents between flakes. However, the specific heat can still be measured when the thermal connection between flakes is very weak. While existing attacks focus on directly inputting malicious examples into models, our research explores a new type of attack where malicious actors use manipulated data generators to manipulate learning. We identify three malicious generator patterns that can effectively manipulate models, and evaluate four deep learning classifiers using two datasets, analyzing the effectiveness of these generators under three different attack types and two data sources. Our findings reveal that generated data can successfully manipulate models, and the efficacy of these generators depends on various factors, including attack type, dataset, and algorithm, with text-based classifiers being more susceptible to attack than image-based ones. Moreover, we identify key limitations of current attacks and propose potential future research directions. This study provides a foundation for further research into advanced adversarial attacks on machine learning systems via manipulated data generators. To address the flatness issue in the early universe, many cosmologists have suggested a period of rapid expansion. However, another approach exists, which proposes that our universe is comprised of a complex, flat lattice structure. Our research delves into three models based on this idea, using the universe's large-scale structure to make predictions. We find that two of these models struggle to explain certain galaxy cluster observations, while a third, dynamically driven model shows more promise, as it's consistent with data from galaxy counts and galaxy rotation tests. Additionally, it's compatible with the universe's large-scale Type Ia supernovae observations up to a certain redshift. We demonstrate that a fourth model, which incorporates dark energy, outperforms the dynamically driven model and becomes the preferred choice, as it's consistent with supernovae data across all redshifts. This is a notable finding, as it's the first flat lattice universe model to successfully explain the observed supernovae data without resorting to dark energy up to a certain redshift. We also discuss potential issues with the universe's small-scale galaxy rotation curve analysis, which could impact the model's performance. We explore three possible ways to address these issues, which further refine the model and result in an even better fit for the supernovae data. Ultimately, our research shows that the model incorporating dark energy is the most suitable choice, as it's capable of explaining a broad range of cosmic phenomena, from the early universe's flatness to the late universe's accelerating expansion, all within a single, consistent framework. We also provide a brief discussion on how to extend the model to include the universe's very early stages. We are confident that our research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the universe and inspire further exploration into the nature of space itself. Many technical details are presented in appendices, along with model parameters, and code for the numerical simulations, which are available on GitHub for public access. We have also prepared educational materials for different age groups, which highlight the research's key findings in an easy-to-understand format.
