A new family of keys-only filters, called xor filters, is introduced, which outperforms Bloom and cuckoo filters in efficiency and speed. Each element in a xor filter is associated with a hash value, and a bit in the filter corresponds to the parity of the hash values for the elements it contains. Insertion involves updating the hash values and recalculating the parities, while membership checks can be done by calculating the parity of the hash values for the given key. This direct approach eliminates the need for additional hash values, reducing memory usage and insertion times. Unlike Bloom filters, which can estimate probabilities of false positives, xor filters provide exact results, similar to cuckoo filters. However, the insertion time of xor filters exceeds that of cuckoo filters, but is faster than previously developed, filter-merge strategies. A key advantage of xor filters is their ability to support element removals through a simple hash-based method, thus allowing existing elements to be removed while opening up space for new elements. This capability is often desired but rarely utilized due to the high removal costs of Bloom and cuckoo filters. Furthermore, a novel class of xor filters called the Avl xor filters has been introduced, which uses self-balancing avl trees to efficiently handle element removals. The development of these filters marks the beginning of a new era where membership-confirmation efficiency and space efficiency are equally valued. As such, these filters are particularly suited for applications requiring the efficient removal of elements, and also when the available memory is a multiple of the word size. The source code for these filters has been made publicly available. Experimental results, including comparisons to state-of-the-art solutions, have been documented, showing that the introduced xor filters achieve a balance between space efficiency and insertion times, while offering the added convenience of efficient element removal capabilities. The introduced xor filters can be categorized into two types, named xor and mod xor, which are based on the hash function used. Specifically, the xor and mod xor filters outperform the cuckoo filters in terms of space efficiency and insertion times, while offering a balance similar to the Bloom filters. In particular, the xor and mod xor filters achieve a 2x space savings over the Bloom filters at the same insertion speeds, while allowing for exact false positive rates similar to the Bloom filters. Additionally, the membership checking times of the introduced xor and mod xor filters are comparable to those of the Bloom filters. Deep learning models heavily rely on extensive training, but face a major obstacle due to the massive computational requirements.  In response, various pruning techniques have been developed to compress models and reduce computational costs, allowing them to be trained on devices with limited memory.  However, existing pruning methods are limited in their applicability as they only support specific pruning types and are incompatible with many popular deep learning frameworks.  Moreover, the majority of previous studies have focused on evaluating the accuracy of compressed models on specific classification tasks, but have neglected to consider their impact on computational costs.  In our study, we introduce ClickTrain, a novel end-to-end deep learning training framework that integrates a fine-grained pruning method to strike a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency.  By preserving the original model architecture during the pruning process, ClickTrain offers precise control over the pruning schedule and allows for the removal of unnecessary neurons.  Furthermore, our method is adaptable to various pruning techniques and can be applied to complex deep learning models without modification.  Through thorough evaluations on widely-used image classification datasets, we demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of ClickTrain, which achieves a 2.5 times speed-up and 0.5% improvement in accuracy compared to the original models.  Additionally, our framework is capable of achieving state-of-the-art performance on mobile hardware while minimizing computational costs.  Notably, ClickTrain prunes up to 90% of the neurons on edge devices while maintaining comparable accuracy to the original models.  Our framework also surpasses existing methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency, and serves as an open-source resource for the deep learning community.  ClickTrain's source code is available at https://github.com/whaiwhai/ClickTrain.  Future upgrades to the framework will be detailed on the website.  In the future, we intend to expand ClickTrain to support other types of deep learning models and prune methods, and will explore its application on other devices such as mobile and IoT devices.  Additionally, we will develop a pruning method that adapts to changing environments in real-world applications.  Our long-term goal is to establish ClickTrain as a widely-adopted deep learning training framework that can be easily integrated into various deep learning libraries.  In the process, we will make regular updates on the progress of ClickTrain at the provided website.  In the end, our framework will be deployed as an open-source tool for the deep learning community.  Our website will serve as the central hub for updates on ClickTrain, and will be regularly maintained

We have established that the modal version of the distributive complete Lambek calculus has a non-empty model when its axioms for modal operators are omitted, and we have identified a specific interpretation that supports this conclusion. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the calculus is not only closed under the usual compositional operation but also invariant under modal transformations. Additionally, we have found a formula for each modal degree of a given formula, and we have shown that the calculus has a saturated model. Moreover, we have identified a formula for each degree of provability in the calculus, and we have proven that the calculus has a forcing model. These results are complemented by examples illustrating cases of non-existence of certain types of models. Specifically, we have provided examples showing that the calculus does not have a modal product model, a modal sheaf model, a modal multiplicative conjunctive modal modal addition model, or a modal S4-like modal addition model. Lastly, we have proposed potential research directions based on these counterexamples. (This work was previously published in arXiv:2101.006399.)

The 2015 detection of a gravitational wave from a binary black hole merger by LIGO has led to a new era of multi-messenger astronomy. Future detections are expected to include the merger of neutron stars and black holes, producing distinctive gravitational waves reflecting various physical aspects of these events. Identifying these events in the noisy gravitational wave data is a daunting task, but essential for enabling multi-messenger observations. We propose a new approach based on a deep learning network, trained on simulated signals, that can distinguish real events from background noise. Additionally, our method can differentiate between various types of binary mergers, and even extract information about their orientation and spin. We also investigate how our approach can be improved by incorporating more realistic simulations of the merging neutron stars and black holes. Our study demonstrates that these events will enable more accurate and detailed inferences about the binary neutron star merger process, and the physics of neutron stars, as well as providing new insights into the rotation and gravitational redshift of neutron stars. We make our code and simulation tools publicly available to facilitate future detections and studies. A transiting exoplanet, identified as a hot Jupiter, has been found in the TOI-5542 system by the Kepler space telescope's data reuse initiative. This planet, with a radius of 1.23 Earth radii and an orbital period of 85 days, primarily orbits TOI-5542, revolving around it as it moves through the system. Analysis of the host star, located 393.4 parsecs from Earth, revealed it to be an older star, with properties including a solar-like effective temperature, low metal content, and a low rotation speed. This planet, with a mass similar to that of Jupiter, likely formed quickly and has since undergone minimal changes, making it an ancient hot Jupiter. This discovery adds to the small collection of ancient hot Jupiters known and helps to better understand the formation and evolution of such planets. Further research on this system, particularly through the observation of a possible second planet, could provide valuable insights into its unique characteristics and the dynamics of the TOI-5542 planetary system. This discovery was made possible through the continued analysis of Kepler data, thanks to the space telescope's extended mission, and supports the ongoing search for ancient hot Jupiters and other exoplanets in the program. Additionally, observations by the TESS and Skymapper telescopes have facilitated further research on the TOI-5542 system, with the goal of gaining more in-depth knowledge of this ancient hot Jupiter and its accompanying features. This discovery contributes to our understanding of the ancient hot Jupiters among the known planets and paves the way for the discovery of more such planets, particularly those with smaller radii, through the continued observation of Kepler data and the program's ongoing initiatives. We introduce a new primal-dual algorithm to solve complex optimization problems with multiple choice options and constraints that change over time. At each time step, the decision-maker selects the optimal choice that maximizes a reward function while adhering to given constraints. Leveraging the Lagrangian multiplier technique, our approach converts this optimization problem into a sequence of constrained Markov decision processes. Our primal-dual method combines simultaneous optimization and policy selection, allowing it to be fully informed. In situations where perfect information is not attainable, our method incorporates concepts from one-step look ahead and entropy regularization to ensure a more balanced solution. By analyzing the algorithm's performance, we establish conditions under which it achieves optimal outcomes and prove that alternative methods like value function approximation and policy synthesis result in suboptimal performance compared to our primal-dual algorithm when operating in unknown environments. Finally, we showcase the efficacy of our algorithm through numerical demonstrations, including applications in online portfolio management and online supply chain management. These examples highlight the advantages of our algorithm over alternative methods that are more suitable for known environments but less effective in unknown environments. Our research has potential implications for various real-world contexts where decision-makers must navigate complex, ever-changing environments characterized by multiple choice options and evolving constraints. This study presents a thorough review of the most recent advancements in the recognition of offline handwritten mathematical expressions. Our review includes an analysis of the distinct characteristics of mathematical handwriting, an examination of the most commonly used evaluation metrics, a detailed survey of traditional and cutting-edge recognition techniques, including the use of Leabra, a neural-based software, and a discussion of the additional challenges posed by complex mathematical expressions. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and the combination of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and LSTM for handwritten mathematical recognition. Additionally, our findings reveal that the application of mathematical recognition to tasks such as searching document contents, translating documents, and extracting information is highly beneficial. Our research also explores the potential of Leabra and LSTM-CNN for complex mathematical recognition and highlights the significance of visual and linguistic features for this complex notation. Our research data and models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/aman211/mathchr. This study was partially supported by a grant from the Council for Inclusive Technology Implementation (CITI). Our research acknowledges the contributions of MathDoc and LaTeChto, systems for converting mathematical documents, and the influence of recent advancements in vision and language models on handwritten mathematical recognition. Our study culminates in a framework for complex mathematical recognition by integrating the strengths of different techniques. Our research demonstrates the recognition capabilities of Leabra and LSTM-CNN on the DMC dataset and highlights the challenges of applying this technique to other datasets. Our research evaluates the performance of different techniques using the widely used evaluation metrics and notes that the integration of LSTM and CNN may be surpassed by other methods that employ feature extraction and ensemble techniques. Our study contrasts the approaches of supervised and unsupervised machine learning and discusses the feasibility of converting LaTeChto and MathDoc, two renowned systems for converting mathematical documents, into trainable models. Our research identifies the key challenges of converting these systems and proposes solutions to overcome these obstacles. Our study presents two novel approaches, named Mathformer and MathTransformer, for converting the contents of mathematical documents. Our research demonstrates the conversion of these contents into readable text and highlights the distinct features of each approach. Our study acknowledges the contributions of two systems, MathDoc and LaTeChto, and presents two evaluation metrics for assessing their performance. The dynamic behavior of interconnected systems is characterized by the interplay of components on various scales, affecting their function and stability. To uncover the underlying mechanisms of these interactions, researchers analyze the patterns of activity within systems in real-time, often using advanced statistical methods. This work takes a different approach, focusing on the unpredictability of interactions within large networks by measuring the degree of irregular behavior in their nodes. Our analysis reveals that this irregularity is not randomly distributed and instead follows a specific, scale-dependent pattern, which varies depending on the network's architecture and the type of connections between nodes. By using this information, we can distinguish between natural and induced disturbances in these systems, such as those caused by external stressors or errors in the network's operation. Ultimately, this research enables us to identify the areas of a network that play a critical role in its functioning and understand how to modify or control their behavior to maintain network stability. To illustrate this methodology, we conducted an in-depth analysis of two systems: a group of fireflies communicating through bioluminescence and a technological network utilizing radio frequency signals. Our results demonstrate the practical application of this approach, allowing us to pinpoint the sources of instability in these systems and even remotely calm disturbed nodes in the firefly network. This research provides a framework for other researchers and practitioners to apply this methodology on a wide range of networks and offers a new perspective on the dynamic behavior of interconnected systems. Our analysis is based on a theoretical framework and is accompanied by extensive numerical simulations, which are available along with the paper in a public repository. Additionally, we have developed an interactive tool allowing users to explore the application of this methodology in their own research. Our method can be employed online for over 20 example networks, including various biological and technological networks, as well as random networks with scale-free and hierarchical architectures. This enables researchers to gain a deeper understanding of the variability of interactions in complex networks and potentially identify common patterns across different systems. By doing so, we can gain a better insight into how these systems function and how to control their behavior. Our work also raises fundamental questions, such as the source of the irregular patterns in these systems and the inherent limitations of these networks affecting their behavior. These open issues represent significant challenges for future research, which could lead to groundbreaking advances in our understanding of dynamic networks and potentially even technological applications. Our code and simulated data are available for other researchers to verify our results and build upon our findings. The Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning structure has been widely adopted due to its ability to learn both the policy and the value function simultaneously. However, it often faces the challenge of exploring the action space efficiently, particularly in high-action-space scenarios. The Q-function's overestimation issue also poses a significant problem, as it can lead to premature policy convergence. This research aims to address these limitations by integrating Actor-Critic models with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) techniques. The incorporation of HMC enables more effective exploration of the action space through the creation of distributions tailored to the Q-function. Furthermore, by utilizing the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, the overestimation issue associated with the Q-function can be mitigated. The integration of HMC techniques was applied to various Reinforcement Learning tasks, including continuous action spaces, and demonstrated improved performance in a simulated robotic environment. The results showed that the combination of Actor-Critic models and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo techniques (AHC) yielded a substantial enhancement of 25.8% and 53.6% over the conventional actor-critic method in terms of success rate and training time, respectively. Our underwater robot navigation system has been enhanced with an advanced method for avoiding obstacles, which is based on a layered management approach. This management system utilizes sonar sensors in two ways: giving short-term, immediate directions to the robot in the short term, and providing long-term planning and route adjustment in the long term. In the short term, a dynamic direction-giving system based on the closest sonar reading has been improved with the ability to consider multiple sonar readings simultaneously. This has been achieved by implementing a new calculation method that weighs the distance of objects in a certain area around the robot, effectively simulating a circular field of view with varying sensitivity to objects. This allows the robot to navigate more effectively, even when there are multiple objects at different distances, and has made the decision-making process more consistent and predictable. As a result, the robot's trajectory is now more stable and less erratic. In the long term, a separate module plans the robot's route in advance, taking into account areas that the short-term system has flagged as potential obstacles. When an obstacle is detected in the short term, the corresponding area is flagged in the long-term manager, which adjusts the robot's navigation accordingly. This has made the robot's navigation highly reliable, with a success rate of over 90% in tests. This approach has also reduced the load on the robot's decision-making system, as the long-term manager only updates the robot's route when there are changes, rather than constantly adjusting the navigation based on new readings. As a result, the robot's navigation is now highly efficient, with a speed of over 0.8 meters per second in tests. This speed is due in part to the long-term manager's ability to anticipate and plan for areas that the short-term system has flagged as potential obstacles in advance, effectively allowing the robot to navigate through complex environments with ease. This approach has also enabled the robot to detect and track targets efficiently, with a success rate of over 80% in tests. The robot's ability to detect and track targets is due in part to the long-term manager's ability to anticipate and plan for areas that the short-term system has flagged as potential targets in advance, effectively allowing the robot to navigate to and track targets with ease. This approach has also made the robot's navigation highly adaptable, with a versatility rating of over 0.9 in tests. This adaptability is due in part to the long-term manager's ability to adjust the robot's navigation based on a wide range of factors, including the detection of obstacles

This is analogous to the Tukey tree, a concept introduced by Jack Good in 1967-68 as a model for a natural number sequence. We propose modifying the Tukey tree to incorporate the Pawlikowski tree, a more dynamic structure whose branches divide at unpredictable intervals, as initially demonstrated in the 1970s by Andrzej Pawlikowski. Our modification will enable the derivation of more precise bounds on the density of $a_n$, specifically that the density is greater than $n^{-1/\log n}$ and less than $n^{-1}/\log n$, demonstrating the equivalence of the Pawlikowski order to the Rudin-Keisler order. We examine certain duality concepts and applications to invariants derived from the minimal free resolution of a polynomial algebra's graded Artinian Gorenstein quotient. Specifically, we investigate the relationship between the Koszul duality of graded Artinian Gorenstein quotients and the duality of the polynomial algebra and its dual. Additionally, we explore the implications of this relationship on the invariants. Moreover, we extend the concepts and methods of Artinian Gorenstein quotients to dualizable and reflexive modules, including those that are not Gorenstein quotients. Based on this generalization, we derive new results and apply them to the invariants of dualizable and reflexive modules. Ultimately, our study aims to understand the relationship between the structure of a module and the information contained in its minimal free resolution. To this end, we combine methods from commutative algebra, duality theory, and invariant theory. The special case of Artinian Gorenstein quotients enables us to derive significant conclusions about the algebra and its invariants, but this case is rather isolated. By generalizing the concepts to dualizable and reflexive modules, we achieve a more versatile approach that can be applied to a broader range of modules. Some of the specific invariants we investigate include the injective dimension, the Buchsbaum-Taylor depth of the socle, the Lichtenbaum-Kune-Miller invariants, the Vermeeren invariants, and the Tor-algebra. In recent years, presence-absence data has experienced significant growth across different scientific and industrial fields due to advances in high-throughput techniques such as mass spectrometry, next-generation sequencing, and others. This surge has been largely driven by the increasing availability and accessibility of such technologies. Presence-absence data represents a type of binary response where each data point can be represented as a binary vector. One key application of such data involves cluster analysis, which enables researchers to gain insights into the composition of samples, distinguish between different groups, and identify potential biomarkers, among other things. Consequently, there is an emerging need to compare and evaluate the various clustering methods available for presence-absence data and to investigate the effectiveness of different optimization approaches. This study utilizes 16 internal indices, including well-established metrics like the Calinski-Harabasz index, as well as more recent proposals such as the Davies-Bouldin index and the topological similarity index. Our analysis involves simulated data sets as well as 16 real-world case studies spanning various applications and dimensions. One key area of investigation involves the performance of different clustering algorithms on presence-absence data sets of different dimensions. Our results demonstrate that the Calinski-Harabasz index and the topological similarity index exhibit the greatest correlation with human evaluation, indicating their potential as reliable evaluation metrics for presence-absence data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the application of presence-absence data to the evaluation of clustering performance is both feasible and beneficial. Additionally, our study highlights the importance of considering both data type and dimensionality when selecting an appropriate clustering algorithm. Finally, our results show that the performance of clustering algorithms can be largely replicated using simulated data, but with some notable exceptions, and that the optimal clustering solution may vary depending on the index used for evaluation, underscoring the need for comprehensive and diverse testing. Our code and data are publicly available for download at https://github.com/alexandrelp/Presence-Absence-Clustering. This repository includes the R code for the analysis, as well as the presence-absence data sets used in our study. Our software also includes a range of novel clustering algorithms, including the fast and efficient FASTPAC package, as well as a range of other approaches. Additionally, the repository contains a comprehensive guide to the available clustering methods, their underlying algorithms, and our evaluation of their performance based on our analysis. This includes both simulated and real-world data, spanning a range of different dimensions and applications. Consequently, the repository can serve as a valuable resource for researchers

In recent years, salient object detection using RGB and RGB-D data has received significant attention due to its numerous practical applications. However, current methods typically design specific pipelines for each data type, with inconsistencies in their approaches. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a unified framework that effectively tackles both tasks in a unified manner. By leveraging the unique characteristics of each data type, our proposed method extracts rich features from each input, which are then fused and refined to produce the final saliency map. Notably, our method's feature extraction process involves the use of depth information, which is often underutilized in RGB-based methods. Through extensive experimentation, we have found that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, with a notable improvement of 5.53% in terms of the mean average precision index. To validate the efficacy of our proposed method, we have also conducted ablation studies and analyzed its performance on various datasets. The code and datasets used in this study can be accessed via the following repository: https://github.com/zzmztju/SALIENT. Our proposed method has been successfully applied in the creation of an automatic saliency-based image annotation system, which demonstrates the practical applications of this technology. The annotated images can be found at the following repository: https://github.com/zzmztju/saliency_image_annotation. The images annotated by our proposed method have been found to outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques, as well as human annotators, in terms of consistency and accuracy. The findings of this study highlight the potential of salient object detection as a powerful tool for a wide range of computer vision tasks. The integration of depth information has been found to significantly contribute to the performance of this technology, underscoring the importance of utilizing diverse data types to tackle complex computer vision problems. The study's findings have been presented at the 2021 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV). This study presents our approaches to identifying aggressive text on the SemEval 2019 shared task. Our strategy entailed utilizing two distinct methods: a BERT-based model and a support vector machine, to predict the levels of aggression towards a speaker in a given tweet. Our approach first involved converting raw tweets into formal English using a language processing model, then extracting key features from the sentence to present to the BERT model. Our BERT model leveraged a BERT representation of the speaker's language as its primary feature, while our SVM method employed multiple relevant features such as language, speaker-related text, and sentiment or question markers. Our combined system, UM-IU@LING, submitted both entries to the competition. Our BERT entry ranked 15th and our SVM entry ranked 20th, out of 61 and 60 submissions respectively, with an F1 score of 0.7443 for the BERT entry and 0.7344 for the SVM entry. Our entries' performances will be detailed, along with lessons learned and potential areas for improvement. Ultimately, this study aims to contribute to the development of advanced natural language processing capabilities through the application of BERT and other machine learning techniques to real-world text classification problems. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

We establish and confirm a relationship between two types of finite integer sequences: those that adhere to a symmetrical pattern and those that adhere to an antisymmetrical pattern. Specifically, we demonstrate that when an antisymmetrical sequence is divided by a symmetrical sequence, the result often lies within the realm of positive integers or, alternatively, negative integers. Notably, this quotient can also yield fractions if the dividing sequence contains zero values. Building on this discovery, we define a new method of division, termed 'quotient division', and explore its implications. Furthermore, we investigate key properties of these sequences, such as their greatest common divisors, and examine the behavior of a specific mathematical operation when applied to these sequences. Ultimately, our analysis leads to a fundamental generalization. Additionally, we provide examples and counterexamples to illustrate our findings as well as to question our theoretical outcomes. Interestingly, some of our observations led to the realization that certain results could be reduced to known findings in number theory. In particular, our work on the behavior of certain sequences and the resulting formulas bears resemblance to results related to the Riemann Hypothesis. Lastly, our research raises new questions and encourages further exploration. Certain aspects of our study were hindered due to technical limitations, prompting us to offer conjectures and potential areas for future research. In particular, our work on the Distribution of Quotient Values and some related generalizations remains to be fully addressed. Nonetheless, our findings include an exact formula for the first term and a pattern for the subsequent terms, raising questions about the eventual convergence of the sequence. Moreover, we identify an interesting property related to the Fibonacci sequence and propose further investigation. Finally, we present an open problem related to our division theory, specifically the Division Hypothesis, along with an initial investigation of its consequences. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that the behavior of these integer sequences can provide insights into established theorems of number theory, while also presenting new hypotheses and areas for further exploration. In particular, our work on the Riemann Hypothesis and the Fibonacci sequence Conjecture could have significant implications if proven true. Conversely, our research may also lead to the realization that these results are inherently false. In any case, our research presents a new and distinct perspective on these established theorems and presents novel hypotheses and areas for further research. Additionally, certain aspects of our findings are hindered by technical limitations and is contingent on the resolution of certain problems in number theory. Nonetheless, our research offers new insights and presents novel hypotheses and areas

This method, supported by an attention-based saliency estimation technique, enables the model to focus on relevant character information. Our proposed framework comprises three components: a character recognition module, a character generator, and a segmentation module. We validate our approach through experiments on the TS and BA datasets, achieving notable results with reduced training data. We have established a combined approach that links ab initio calculations of atomic nuclei to their corresponding core atomic structures, enabling us to generate accurate predictions of nuclear properties and energy levels using many-body theory. By applying a computationally efficient method to solve the Kohn-Sham equations for the nuclear density and single-particle wave functions, we have developed a technique to calculate the nuclear energy landscape and ground-state characteristics. Specifically, our framework allows us to predict energy levels, transition probabilities, and other nuclear properties within the framework of the relativistic nuclear structure theory, which has been validated through our analysis of the isotonic chains of thorium and uranium. By varying the number of protons and neutrons while keeping the neutron-to-proton ratio constant, we have been able to gain new insights into how nuclei change and transition. Our study has also compared our results to experimental data and found that our predictions are in close agreement with the actual values. Furthermore, our research has revealed that the signed nucleon-nucleon interaction is capable of explaining a range of phenomena, including the light closed-shell and semi-magic closed-shell and deformed shell nuclei. By utilizing our scheme in conjunction with the response function, we have been able to establish a connection between the nuclear structure and the initial and final nuclear states through the collective multipole operators, thereby enabling us to make precise predictions about nuclear transitions and energy spectra based on the nuclear structure principles. Specifically, our approach has allowed us to link the low-energy electromagnetic multipole responses to the corresponding E2 transition strengths and energy spectra, thereby establishing a direct relationship between the nuclear structure and the electromagnetic interaction. Moreover, our study has shown that the monopole component of the nuclear response plays a crucial role in the ground-state deformation, which is in agreement with the traditional nuclear structure theory. By solving the in-medium relativistic nuclear quadratic response equation, we have been able to establish a connection between the longitudinal and transverse response functions of the nucleon and the photon, thereby enabling us to make precise predictions about the double longitudinal and double transverse photoneutron reaction rates and to relate these reaction rates to the corresponding electromagnetic multipole operators. Specifically, our study has shown that the double longitudinal reaction rate is directly linked to the E2 transition strength, while the double transverse reaction rate is linked to the E1 transition strength. Moreover, our research has revealed that the signed nucleon-nucleon interaction is capable of explaining a range of phenomena, including the reaction rates and the deformation of light and semi-magic closed-shell nuclei.

In CPU-based programming, memory management is typically handled by an operating system, but in the context of GPU programming, developers are responsible for memory management as the underlying system. This involves efficiently allocating and deallocating memory to avoid underallocations and allocations that don't stick. To address these issues, a new memory allocator, DynaSOAr, has been developed for Fortran 2003 and C++3.0 on AMD GPUs through the SYCL programming model. This talk will detail how DynaSOAr, which is designed for object-oriented applications, uses a multi-level approach with a dictionary-based memory management system to optimize memory usage and provide features like flexible, fine-grained memory allocation and deallocation, as well as the ability to link Fortran and C++ code through the C++Interop interface. Additionally, DynaSOAr will be compared to the default memory allocator that comes with the Compute Runtime, and support has been added for memory pools and memory management policy to make DynaSOAr a part of the HIP library. Moreover, a significant number of bugs have been fixed, and several features including stack-based memory management, custom memory allocation, and deallocation have been added to DynaSOAr. Finally, the DynaSOAr allocator is now available on GitHub under the permissive MIT-LICENSE and can be used with AMD HIP and SYCL development kits. The investigation into a failed straw, part of the Large Hadron Collider's (LHC) injection system, revealed the presence of a crack located at a 45-degree angle with respect to the straw's axis. To better understand this failure, a computational model was developed to analyze the stress within the straw's material. The results showed that the stress levels were below the detection threshold of available monitoring systems. However, the model's limitations, coupled with uncertainties in material stress calculations, made it difficult to draw more precise conclusions. Nonetheless, the study provided a foundation for further research and suggested implementing regular visual inspections of the straws. Through an iterative process of stress analysis, the risk of new crack development could be minimized. Moreover, the study underscored the significance of considering actual operating conditions in stress calculations, rather than relying on static models. Ultimately, the research highlighted the need for a more in-depth stress analysis, taking into account dynamic factors, to ensure a more comprehensive understanding of the straw's mechanical state. The proposed model could be applied to other components, facilitating a more unified and comprehensive safety assessment for the LHC's Liquefied Nitrogen Transfer system. The work presented here could serve as a starting point for a broader safety analysis, encompassing not only the LHC's strays but also other pipe systems, through a standardized procedure. The proposed approach could also be adapted for other infrastructure and industry applications, where similar risks may exist. We introduce a framework for quantifying the reliability of probabilistic circuits when applied to specific problem domains under uncertain data. Our approach involves initial research into a related optimization problem, which we term the probabilistic constraint relaxation problem (PCRP). By solving PCRP, we can ensure that the solution to a particular Bayesian learning or optimization task remains within a certain margin of error in the solution space. The PCRP appears to be a complex problem, but we prove that it can be tackled more efficiently than traditional constraint relaxation methods. Specifically, we show that PCRP can be solved by scaling polynomially with the number of constraints when working with probabilistic circuits. Our framework has significant potential for applications in various fields, such as machine learning, optimization, and signal processing, and we illustrate its usefulness with two practical examples. Further details are available in our supplementary materials. Additionally, we have made the corresponding code available at https://github.com/robber/pcrp. We explore the occurrence of Bloch oscillations in superfluids/neutron stars consisting of up-down quark matter with a specific type of interaction, focusing on the dynamics governed by the Phasespace Eilenberger equation for non-condensate quasiparticles. Our analysis begins with a detailed examination of the equation's properties and analytical solutions in a constant magnetic field, before moving on to numerical simulations of the oscillatory process. These oscillations are discovered to be significantly impacted by the non-condensate quasiparticle spectrum and magnetic field strength. Moreover, we find that an initial spatial distribution of oscillatory amplitude can develop into a complex pattern over time, influenced by the quasiparticle properties and magnetic field. Finally, we investigate the behavior of oscillations when the system is placed in a state of non-zero temperature, revealing a change in the oscillatory pattern and amplitude due to thermal effects. Our analysis provides a framework for future numerical studies of the oscillatory process within the up-down quark matter phase of superfluids/neutron stars. The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) at the heart of the Milky Way is an intricate network of gas that surrounds the Compact Radio Source. By analyzing radio continuum data from ATLASGAL, researchers have derived a two-dimensional radial correlation function to quantify the anisotropic mass distribution within the CMZ's core area. They compared this approach to other methods, such as Gaussian fits and three-dimensional calculations, which all yielded consistent results. The data indicated that the CMZ's mass configuration exhibits a symmetrical north-south pattern with a local density increase of $ \sim 10^{22}$ cm$^{-2}$ in the central 20 parsecs. This pattern is similar to findings from other research and supports theories suggesting that gas in the CMZ is compressed by explosive outbursts originating from the black hole. The study's methodology can be applied to future studies using more sensitive data, which are expected to provide even more detailed insights into the CMZ's mass configuration. The research also suggests that further investigation is necessary to resolve discrepancies between different data sets in the CMZ's mass distribution. We introduce a simple rate-based model that explains how electrons move during high-fluence X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy in materials that contain transition metals. This model doesn't rely on specific physical processes or make detailed assumptions about the interaction between light and matter. It's based solely on the readjustment of the material's electronic equilibrium. We use this model to simulate the time-dependent change in the number of excited electrons in two typical materials near their absorption edges. Our simulation results are in line with the actual experimental data for both silicon-doped diamond and silicon. We compare our model to another model that takes into account all the ways light interacts with matter and find that their predictions are similar. This agreement confirms that the electronic rates of change can effectively describe the sudden change in the electronic equilibrium caused by high-fluence X-ray pulses. This understanding is crucial for interpreting high-fluence X-ray ABS data and making sense of the observed delay and changes in response. Our model also highlights the importance of knowing the initial electronic state of the material and the duration of the X-ray pulse to accurately analyze the data. Our simulation results are in good agreement with the actual experimental data for both materials, demonstrating the effectiveness of this model. A compact and energy-efficient temperature sensor with a wide operating range is presented, featuring a programmable sub-range of -20$^\circ$C to 120$^\circ$C with an adjustable resolution of 0.1 or 0.2 degrees Celsius. The temperature detector includes a PTAT current generator, a short and simple Gm-boost circuit, and an event-driven SAR ADC that incorporates a fully-balanced switch topology to minimize switching noise and improve data accuracy. With a 1.80V supply voltage, the proposed temperature detector achieves a conversion error of less than 0.24 degrees Celsius, a 3.5-bit effective resolution, and a data rate of up to 200 kHz, all within a 0.13mm$^2$ area. To expand its applicability, the design can be optimized for a 0.6V to 1.80V supply voltage range, resulting in a coarser resolution of 1.0 degrees Celsius with a conversion error of approximately 1.4 degrees Celsius and a data rate of up to 100 kHz for the same area. This versatile temperature detector features a power consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion, making it suitable for a wide range of integrated and stand-alone temperature measurement applications. Experimental results demonstrate that the temperature sensor functions accurately across various supply voltages, even when subject to noise and demonstrating temperature-dependent nonlinearity (TDNL) with a maximum error of 1.4 degrees Celsius. Additionally, the designer has developed a calibration technique to minimize temperature-dependent nonlinearity (TDNL) that may arise in certain process variants, ultimately resulting in a temperature sensor with an error of no more than 0.24 degrees Celsius. Finally, the authors have developed a simple calibration method to minimize any potential temperature-dependent nonlinearity (TDNL) that may be present in certain integrated circuit designs. We present a novel algorithm, the Distorted Resolvent Method (DRM), which efficiently generates Nash equilibria for a broad category of Nash games. DRM's utility lies in its ability to replicate the outcomes of any continuous exact Newton-type method, thereby encompassing numerous existing proposals. Furthermore, DRM has two key advantages: it can distill the computational complexities of other algorithms, such as condensing redundant operations; and it can introduce distortions to accelerate convergence, similar to complexity-reducing techniques. We outline two specific implementations of DRM, one that achieves superlinear convergence and another with a simplified computational requirement. We also examine the performance of these implementations, alongside two other prominent algorithms, in a stochastic Nash game applied to a power grid problem. Interestingly, while all methods yielded comparable outcomes in terms of social welfare, our implementations of DRM demonstrated superior computational efficiency. Consequently, DRM offers a versatile approach for generating Nash equilibria, while also providing valuable insights for designing low-complexity algorithms. Additionally, our findings suggest that the outcomes of various game-theoretic algorithms may be more analogous than previously thought. As such, our work could serve as a comprehensive framework for algorithm design in Nash games. Furthermore, DRM may also be applicable to other areas, such as optimization and stochastic processes, through simple modifications. We conducted extensive simulations to investigate the emergence of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) as a potential dark energy component in the Universe, employing the PopSyCLE merger rate calculator. PBH dark energy, a hypothetical phenomenon, could explain cosmic acceleration and even the Universe's late-time disappearance. Our simulations aimed to model the PBH density evolution, facilitated by PopSyCLE's $\rho(t)$ output, rather than the merger rates typically used. To validate our approach, we analyzed the astrophysical implications of our simulations, specifically examining the PBH feeble gravitational lensing signal and the impact on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation. Our results reveal a minor CMB anisotropy reduction (~5%) and a considerable increase in the lensing signal compared to standard Lambda-CDM models, primarily due to the long-lived PBHs. To further refine our methodology, we incorporated PopSyCLE's time-dependent PBH abundance output, allowing us to derive an equation of state for PBH dark energy. Our research demonstrates that PBH dark energy, as modeled by PopSyCLE, yields a feeble but detectable effect on the CMB lensing and a distinctive signature in the equation of state of dark energy, making it distinguishable from other dark energy models. To facilitate future PBH dark energy searches, we provided the PopSyCLE simulation outputs for various models. We aim to uncover the underlying characteristics of Vision Transformers (ViTs) that distinguish them from traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with the ultimate goal of leveraging these properties to fine-tune and propel ViTs to excellence. To that end, we investigate ViT's behavior using diverse image datasets and pinpoint three essential attributes: robustness to input resolution, sensitivity to input size, and adaptability to input format. Our findings demonstrate that CNNs and ViTs exhibit similar levels of robustness to changes in input resolution but ViTs are more sensitive to alterations in input size, and are also more format-specific than CNNs. Building on these discoveries, we devise two novel self-guided ViT architectures, named 2xViT-32 and 2ViT-32, which integrate double-resolution training and input format adaptation to exploit these properties. Our experiments show that these new models outperform existing ViTs and achieve remarkable improvements across a range of tasks, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, without incurring additional computational costs. Our proposed approach, which we term Property-Aware Model Development, serves as a valuable tool to facilitate the design of ViTs that are both theoretically grounded and empirically effective. This study integrates reversible concealment techniques, including image compression and encryption, utilizing Bayesian Neural Networks. By applying predictive uncertainty quantification, we can assess and control the effectiveness of concealment methods on data that has been intentionally distorted. Our theoretical framework shows that the stochastic nature of Bayesian Neural Networks can achieve reliable data restoration, as long as the quality of the distorted data remains relatively high. However, when the quality significantly declines, the network falls back on a robust but suboptimal restoration approach. To mitigate this issue, we develop an adaptive strategy, allowing the network to switch between a high-quality and a backup restoration method based on the predictive uncertainty. The integrated BNNs are then tested on various distortion methods, including bit-plane masking, discrete cosine transform hiding, and encrypted images, demonstrating the benefits of predictive uncertainty-guided data restoration in challenging concealment scenarios. Furthermore, the integrated BNNs exhibit superior performance in restoring heavily distorted images, as evidenced by our experimental results. This phenomenon is attributed to the presence of magnetic bright spots at the boundaries of larger solar units, such as supergranular cells, with their magnitudes distributed in a power-law fashion. Two theoretical models are proposed to explain this distribution: the first, based on the idea that small magnetic areas are contained within larger ones, resulting in a distinct bi-partite frequency pattern as their sizes ratio varies; the second, incorporating the idea of magnetic bright spots as isolated loops, with their persistence times distributed according to a power-law, leading to a bi-partite distribution as well. Both models are supported by numerical simulations, and while neither can be exclusively correct, our analysis of solar image data reveals a strong correlation with the first model, suggesting that the bi-partite frequency distribution is a manifestation of the hierarchical structure of the sun's magnetic field. This discovery provides direct empirical evidence of the sun's magnetic field topology and its implications for understanding solar activity. Moreover, this study provides a framework for testing theoretical models of solar behavior with observational data, offering a new perspective on the sun's behavior. Our analysis builds on prior research, quantifying how human decisions are influenced by past observations. Human behavior, observed through both laboratory studies and real-world applications like financial markets, exhibits complex patterns that are often beyond current model capabilities. By applying a straightforward statistical test, we evaluate the consistency of human responses to changing economic conditions, revealed through a long-term study of stock market activities by Kyle and Becker (1997). To facilitate comparison with their data, we provide an implementation of their study design in Python. We suggest a new theoretical framework for shadow matter, specifically for milli-magnetic monopoles, and explore its implications for the phenomenon of persistent cosmic magnetic fields. The concept of quantum field localization in the monopole's core, combined with the influence of the Weinberg operator, leads to the generation of the quantum field's virtually paired state as a macroscopic entity. This process is driven by the magnetic field's presence and, in turn, the monopole itself becomes immersed in the magnetic field, thus absorbing some magnetic flux. As a result, we observe that the monopole resists displacement by an external magnetic field, and we propose that the monopole's interaction with the magnetic field could provide a possible mechanism for the sustained presence of cosmic magnetic fields in the early universe. Furthermore, we propose that the monopole, once created, could serve as a stable seed for magnetic field generation, and we estimate that, for a particular dark matter mass range ($10^{-18}\mathrm{eV}$ to $10^{-16}\mathrm{eV}$), we can generate sufficient dark matter to account for the universe's dark matter content. Additionally, we discuss the potential detectability of these milli-magnetic monopoles and suggest that they could be captured and studied using advanced technologies such as the Large Hadron Collider or dedicated capture facilities. Finally, we outline the possible implications of discovering these monopoles for our understanding of particle physics and the fundamental laws of nature. The estimated mass range of these milli-magnetic monopoles ($10^{-3}$ GeV to $10^{-1}$ GeV) coincides with that of the LHC's detection capabilities, and we predict that these monopoles should be produced at a rate comparable to that of top quark pairs. Therefore, we propose that the LHC could either detect these monoPOles or provide upper limits on their production that would significantly exceed current expectations based on standard monopole models. Moreover, we demonstrate that these milli-magnetic monopoles could naturally arise within the framework of symmetry-breaking and that their shadow matter properties could be characterized through measurements of the monopole's self-interaction, thereby providing a novel way to understand the phenomenon of matter shadowing. The estimated cross-section for monoPOle production should be detectable if the monoPOles' masses lie in the lower end of the estimated range, and we could set upper limits on monoPOle production if the monoPOles' masses lie in the higher end of the estimated range.

Predicting spatial and temporal climate change with limited data is a complex issue.
Research has shown that deep learning models can effectively address this problem.
To improve the accuracy of climate prediction, we developed a cutting-edge Transformer model with a
multi-scale, shifted window cross-attention mechanism.
Our proposed method leverages the use of a single global feature in the encoder and a multi-scale
Transformer decoder with the shifted window cross-attention method.
We tested this approach using the Climate Time Series dataset, comparing it to several established
models and found that it outperformed them significantly, with an average improvement of 6.3% over
the second best method. Additionally, we found that a pre-trained model could be effectively utilized
as a feature extractor, resulting in even better outcomes. Our source code is available for review.

We've explored the implementation of $S_3$ symmetry in three-Higgs-doublet models to investigate their ability to provide a dark matter particle. Our models have a minimal dark matter nature in two cases: one that is completely stable and two that is metastable. In the first case, we have a model with a dark matter particle composed of fermions that interacts via Yukawa coupling with two heavy pseudoscalar bosons, resulting in a dark matter coefficient $c$ that can be used to test dark matter's existence via direct detection experiments. Our analysis shows that dark matter particles with a mass range of $10$-$$100\,\text{GeV}$ can be ruled out due to an anomaly in the $\mu\to e\gamma$ process, but we find that the anomaly can be avoided in the second case, where the dark matter particle is composed of fermions and interacts via a heavy pseudoscalar boson, resulting in a dark matter coefficient $c$ that is larger than a previously established lower limit. In both cases, we have established the dark matter particle's stability or metastability using a quantum number defined by the $S_3$ symmetry. Additionally, we have verified that the natural alignment of the three Higgs doublets, which is required for a natural fermi-scale electroweak symmetry breaking, does not significantly impact our results. In the metastable case, we have also shown that the dark matter particle's lifetime is much longer than the age of the universe. Furthermore, we have used the velocity distribution of galaxy clusters to set an upper limit on the dark matter particle's lifetime and found that a particular parameter choice results in a dark matter particle with a lifetime exceeding the age of the universe by orders of magnitude. In both cases, we have also shown that the dark matter particle's electric dipole moment is large and sensitive to its mass and the parameters of the three-Higgs-doublet model, making it amenable to detection in experiments that search for dark matter. In addition, we have established a set of conditions under which the hypothesis is certain to apply. These findings provide further evidence for the hypothesis and shed light on the entanglement properties of complex higher-dimensional systems. They also have implications for the creation of Bell inequalities, which could be useful in future experiments. At the minimum, our results confirm that the hypothesis is true in situations involving four particles in specific arrangements. To maintain this balance, the cell regulates it by controlling when and how ions flow in. This thesis explores ways to model this regulatory system using a complex mathematical model, which includes a special constraint to prevent overcharging. This constraint is particularly challenging because it depends on the solution in a complex way, making it difficult to analyze. To address this issue, the thesis presents three different approaches to deal with this complexity, all of which involve approximating the constraint in different manners. Ultimately, the models developed in this research provide valuable insights into the mathematical problem and potentially offer new perspectives for understanding substance transport in cells. Furthermore, these models could be adapted to address congestion control in computer networks, which poses a similar optimization challenge. By optimizing the models, it may be possible to design more efficient systems, whether biological or man-made. The results presented in this thesis represent a significant step towards this goal. Several numerical test cases are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the models and illustrate the trade-offs involved in approximating the complex constraint. Additionally, the thesis includes a comprehensive review of the relevant mathematical theories and provides a clear, step-by-step guide to solving the optimization problem. This study introduces a new approach to facilitate dependency discovery in complex financial systems by leveraging network motif analysis. In contrast to traditional methods that focus on long-term, stable relationships, this approach enables the identification of shorter-term, latent connections among financial entities. Our analysis, applied to the S&P 500 stock prices over various time periods, reveals multiple network motifs that are significantly associated with future stock price movements. Interestingly, our results demonstrate that the most valuable information for investors can often be found in less stable, short-term patterns, whereas the same does not apply to certain long-term motifs. Furthermore, by combining the predictions derived from different network motifs, along with their respective durations, we achieve improved performance. Our methodology, along with the associated gains, can inspire the development of more effective financial forecasting strategies. Related information, along with the used code, is accessible via an online repository. Our analysis contributes to the existing literature by providing new insights into the application of network motif analysis in financial markets and by suggesting a versatile, flexible framework for financial forecasting. Additionally, our work has potential applications in various domains beyond financial markets, such as discovering significant patterns in genomic data. In summary, our research presents a new approach to discovering meaningful patterns in complex data, along with the associated benefits, and showcases its application on financial markets although it can be applied to other domains. Researchers have made a confirmed detection of a unique astrophysical phenomenon involving the merger of two compact stars: a white dwarf and a neutron star. This event serves as the progenitor for Type Ia supernovae, and similar outcomes can occur when a neutron star or white dwarf merges with a black hole. This study examines the characteristics of a newly observed event, a white dwarf merging with a stellar mass black hole, utilizing data from the Zwicky Transient Facility. An analysis of the event's light curve reveals two distinct phases of emission, separated by a dark period. An analysis of the second emission phase indicates it shares similarities with the post-merger emission of neutron star-black hole mergers in terms of its spectral properties and temporal duration. However, key differences exist, including the second emission phase being both longer and brighter in the case of the white dwarf-black hole merger. Spectral modeling of the first emission phase indicates it may be the result of a cooling envelope, and this process could be accompanied by a significant mass transfer from the white dwarf to the black hole. This mass transfer, estimated to be approximately 0.16 solar masses, occurs shortly after the white dwarf's arrival at the black hole's Roche lobe, leading to the white dwarf's disruption. This disruption, along with the white dwarf's original material, gives rise to the second emission phase, which is identified as a metal-rich outflow. This event stands out as the first observed merger of a white dwarf with a black hole, and it offers valuable insights into the potential emissions following a white dwarf's merger with a black hole, a process that could give rise to the iconic Type Ia supernovae. This research has significant implications for understanding the emissions resulting from such mergers, including those leading to supernovae of type Ia, and it provides a framework for future analysis of similar events detected through the Zwicky Transient Facility. Profiling has become a crucial tool for optimizing various computer systems, yet current dataset profilers have significant limitations. They can only provide general information about datasets and do not take into account the specific characteristics of a particular dataset, such as its size, structure, and content. This is because most datasets are too large to be entirely loaded into a profiler's memory, forcing it to rely on random sampling to gather information. However, this approach can lead to inaccurate results, as the profiler may only encounter a tiny fraction of the dataset, and the resulting profile may not accurately represent the entire dataset. Moreover, random sampling does not guarantee the inclusion of important information, such as outliers, which can provide valuable insights into a dataset. In this study, we argue that a more effective approach is needed and propose a new profiling method called PartProf, which is designed to optimize a particular dataset. PartProf is based on two key techniques: (1) a fast and efficient algorithm for dividing a dataset into smaller, manageable pieces, and (2) a novel evaluation metric that assesses the diversity of these pieces and identifies outliers. Our results demonstrate that PartProf is superior to existing profilers and can be adapted to various optimization tasks with minimal modifications. Additionally, PartProf is accompanied by an open-source toolkit that can be used to create customized profilers for specific datasets. Our research offers a flexible and efficient approach to dataset profiling, and we hope that our toolkit will serve as a valuable resource for other researchers. The entangled spinor interferometer is a cutting-edge device that has surpassed traditional interferometers in precision, with the ability to detect minute gravitational waves. By utilizing the entangled state's unique properties, the device can optimize wave function overlap during interference, outperforming classical combinations. However, these optimizations are hindered when measuring apparatus noise limits detection accuracy. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach has been developed for creating customized quantum states within the entangled system. The method involves introducing controlled losses and entanglement levels to enable seamless transition between different quantum states, with the ability to tailor these states for both ground motion detection and extreme gravitational wave detection. The introduction of customized quantum states has enabled detection beyond traditional interferometer limitations, with a notable gain of over 90% in the latter case. The developed technique also enables rapid switching between different quantum states, with a speed that outperforms previous methods. We have established two sets of estimates for the initial eigenvalue of the nonlinear Robin eigenvalue problem. This problem involves finding the first eigenvalue of a specific nonlinear operator. Our initial estimate assumes a Siudeste- type condition, resulting in an approximation of the eigenvalue. By satisfying a modified Bakry-Emery condition, a more precise lower bound can be obtained. Both conditions were developed in reference to a recent study by Daskalopoulos and Vazquez. This work was motivated by the analysis of a related initial value problem, specifically the radial $p$-Laplace equation. Our estimates have significant implications for the study of standing waves under specific boundary conditions. Furthermore, our findings provide insight into the long-term behavior of solutions to the related initial value problem. Notably, our estimates imply the existence of wave forms that maintain their original shape over extended periods, even in the presence of a nonlinear Robin boundary condition. Ultimately, our work allows us to explore the relationship between the eigenvalue approximation and the Hausdorff dimension of the omega limit set of a solution's graph, a parameter that is influenced by the eigenvalue. This result was previously demonstrated using a different approach in reference [20]. Our approach offers an alternative solution to this problem.

Recent advancements in Deep Learning technology have led to the development of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), which can learn complex representations from graph-structured data. Despite the success of GCNNs, the underlying theoretical foundation is poorly understood, particularly in regards to the GCNN convolutional layer. A new study aims to clarify the GCNN foundation by employing Matched Filtering, a well-established signal processing technique. By using this approach, the analysis provides a precise interpretation of the GCNN convolutional layer and reveals that the popular Graph Attention Mechanism represents an efficient implementation of this concept. Furthermore, the analysis leads to the development of a novel GCNN architecture, Asymmetric GCNNs, which demonstrate superior performance and greater interpretability compared to existing benchmarks. The findings of this study can serve as a foundation for future GCNN research and enable the creation of more transparent and understandable machine learning systems. This setup avoids interference between tasks by separating them, but also makes it difficult to share knowledge. Our study investigates how to effectively prevent interference from occurring in this scenario. To overcome this, we introduced a new method that allows modular agents to share information across similar tasks through a process called similarity-based transfer. Our results show that this approach can partially prevent a negative effect of destructive interference, causing a minor slowdown of around 1.4 times in comparison to a single-task training. Additionally, we discovered that similarity-based transfer can also improve learning when there is no destructive interference by increasing the speed by 4.3 times compared to independently trained agents. Our research also included the development of a tool to automatically identify similar tasks, which allows the transfer of knowledge without manual human input. Recommender systems are divided into two categories: direct and indirect recommendations. Direct recommendations involve suggesting specific items, while indirect recommendations involve providing general guidelines for users. Cooperating filtering (CF) is a well-known and effective method of providing indirect recommendations by predicting user preferences based on similar users. Recent advancements in CF have developed more accurate prediction models, but these methods overlook the inherent groupings in user and item interactions, underutilize available information, and overcomplicate the prediction process. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach that uses biclusters to predict user preferences. Each bicluster consists of a group of users with similar preferences and the items they agree on. Our approach predicts user ratings by selecting the bicluster with the closest agreement to the target user and averaging the ratings of the shared items within that bicluster. We also developed two bicluster construction methods that utilize user and item interaction matrices to identify naturally occurring groups. One method uses a combination of sparsity and similarity measures to construct biclusters while considering the unique characteristics of each user and item. Another method uses collaborative filtering and matrix factorization to construct biclusters while considering the inherent subjectivity of user preferences. We tested our approach on three real-world datasets and compared it to six state-of-the-art methods, including single cluster-based CF and multi-scale CF using deep learning and random biclusters. Our results show that our approach outperforms these methods on all datasets, achieving a significant improvement in predictive accuracy for sparse and differential datasets. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ahmed-omar/User-Specific-Bicluster-CF. Our approach offers several key advantages, including the ability to handle sparse and differential user preferences, the flexibility to incorporate subjectivity, and the ability to group users and items together to enhance prediction accuracy. While CF methods are often seen as indirect and simplistic, our approach demonstrates the potential to outperform more complex methods, highlighting the importance of addressing the inherent complexities of user preferences. Our findings suggest that CF methods can be effective in predicting user preferences, and our contributions offer several novel solutions to addressing the challenges of sparse, differential, and subjective user preferences in recommender systems. Our approach can be applied to other CF methods to enhance prediction accuracy and provide more informative guidelines for users and items. In contrast, this study introduces a more comprehensive model, known as active inference, which posits that data generation and algorithm activity are interconnected. Building on this framework, we develop a method to determine the most effective actions for independent robot navigation using only a low-resolution image. While this approach yields accurate predictions, its computational requirements prove too substantial for practical use in mobile robots. Consequently, we adapt a widely employed collision avoidance algorithm and integrate it within a new version of the active inference framework. In this modified framework, actions are evaluated based on their likelihood given previous observations, as well as the algorithm's prior knowledge. This method enables low-resolution image processing and efficient action selection, facilitating reliable independent navigation. Experimental results demonstrate that the newly designed system successfully navigates through varied environments while avoiding obstacles. Furthermore, comparisons with state-of-the-art collision avoidance methods reveal that our approach outperforms these methods in terms of proximity to obstacles. This paper tackles a previously unaddressed challenge in transportation research, namely incident recognition on dynamic networks. To address this, we've developed a sophisticated approach that utilizes real-time traffic data to identify incidents from historical traffic information. Specifically, we convert the dynamic network into a real-valued temporal graph, where node features represent road conditions and edge features correspond to spatial connectivity. Our proposed method, incident_detection_temporal_graph, leverages a graph neural network to recognize incident patterns by analyzing a specified time period before the incident, as well as the road segments involved. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments using data from the North Jutland Police Department in Denmark, analyzing both micro and macro incident recognition scenarios. Our results indicate that our method outperforms existing techniques, achieving a recall of 0.8136 for macro recognition. Notably, our approach offers several key advantages, including the ability to recognize incidents not directly linked to traffic incidents, as well as providing more accurate incident types by incorporating road segment features. We explore how a strong shock wave and a spherically expanding gas cloud interact in an uneven medium with varying density. Our research indicates that when a high-pressure gas cloud collapses under the force of its own gravity, surrounded by an outward flow of gas driven by pressure, conditions are set for a powerful shock wave to form and propagate. This shock wave will subsequently interact with the surrounding medium, producing an outward-moving pressure wave. Our key findings reveal two distinct stages of expansion. In the initial phase, the pressure waves from individual scattering events overlap, resulting in a predominantly radial pressure distribution. Conversely, in the late stage, these pressure waves superimpose in a more complex manner, ultimately giving rise to a power-law index when measuring pressure ($\propto r^{-3}$). Notably, this later stage contrasts with the commonly held hypothesis of pressure inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the center. Additionally, our research uncovers a previously unacknowledged nonradial velocity component, as well as a previously unrecognized energy flow associated with the shock wave. Our estimates suggest that when a gas cloud with a mass equivalent to 10 solar masses collapses under the force of its own gravity, approximately 30% of the initial kinetic energy will be converted into radiation energy. Finally, we outline two distinct scenarios for the final outcome of this gravitational collapse, including one where the shock wave triggers a bright supernova explosion and another quieter scenario where the shock wave slowly releases energy over an extended period without a supernova explosion. In either case, as the cloud collapses, the characteristic time of the explosion or energy release perfectly matches the predictions of the classic model. Our research provides a definitive explanation to two longstanding questions in astrophysics - the bright supernovae of low and intermediate mass stars (the SN Ia problem) and the soft X-ray and EUV background (the SN Ia problem of light elements). Our research further reveals that only a very narrow mass range (1.0 M_sun < M < 1.1 M_sun) will yield the necessary energy to explain the SN Ia phenomenon.
