The growing presence of AI systems in everyday life is undeniable, from consumer applications to critical industries, where they make pivotal decisions affecting people's lives. While AI's capabilities are impressive, its inner workings are often inaccessible to users, making necessary AI-driven outputs and actions difficult to comprehend. To address this, the concept of Explainable AI (XAI) has emerged, aiming to improve AI models' transparency and accountability. By empowering stakeholders to grasp AI-driven choices and processes, XAI contributes to trust-building among users, customers, and regulators. Notwithstanding, the XAI community has thus far paid scant attention to its users' needs, focusing instead on improving computational approaches to explainability. To bridge this gap, we advocate for a more user-centered approach, highlighting the importance of Requirements Engineering (RE) in shaping XAI development. Through a systematic literature review of XAI, user-centered design, and RE, we pinpoint key user-related aspects of explainability needs that RE can address. Our empirical study, comprising 15 interviews with domain experts, corroborates the relevance of RE in the XAI context. Moving forward, we outline future research avenues, while emphasizing the urgency of incorporating RE principles to ensure that XAI meets the evolving needs and expectations of AI users. Our position paper positions RE as a vital partner in the XAI community, working to fulfill the needs and desires of AI users regarding explainability. Ultimately, this collaboration will result in more transparent, trustworthy, and accountable AI systems that genuinely serve their human constituencies. Our work has practical implications for XAI researchers, practitioners, and developers, reminding them of their responsibility to consider users' perspectives on explainability, as exemplified by the RE community's longstanding emphasis on user involvement. By adopting this user-centered approach, we can develop explainable AI that genuinely addresses the needs and desires of its stakeholders, thereby fostering deeper user trust in AI through improved transparency and accountability. Our position paper thus calls for an RE-led shift in the XAI community, prioritizing computational methods that better reflect human values and needs, as AI systems' enhanced explainability ultimately redounds to the benefit of their human users and stakeholders. Our position paper has been accepted for publication at the 2022 International Conference on Software Engineering. For over a century, histopathological diagnosis has relied on visual inspections by experienced pathologists.
The process's subjectivity can lead to inconsistent diagnoses, motivating researchers to develop artificial intelligence (AI) for histopathology.
Although numerous studies have explored this field, the limited availability of high-quality, annotated datasets has hindered progress.
To contribute to and compare different approaches, a new dataset called UniToPatho has been created, featuring 1,046 histological samples of colorectal polyps along with detailed annotations and multiple gold-standard evaluations.
This resource, comprising 224 images, is offered for download, allowing researchers to replicate previous findings and test alternative methods.
The UniToPatho dataset is optimized for downstream tasks like polyp classification and adenoma dysplasia assessment, enabling more comprehensive diagnostic AI systems.
The project's website provides supplementary information for those interested in these applications.

We demonstrate a coherence property for the Milnor fiber of a hypersurface isolated singularity following a semistable reduction approach. The coherence property implies that the semistable reduction is uniquely determined, and we also show that the dimension of the semistable reduced fiber is constant across a specific open set in the Milnor fiber. Additionally, we formulate a condition related to the cohomology of the fiber that must be satisfied for the Milnor fiber to be non-coherent. Notably, this condition is related to the cohomology of the fiber in the semistable reduced fiber, and it is satisfied when the singular locus of the fiber is smooth. Moreover, this condition is also satisfied when the singular point of the fiber is coherent. We also explore the cohomology of the fiber in various contexts, such as the case of a degenerate fiber, and the case when the semi-stable reduction is replaced by a formal semistable reduction. Finally, we conjecture that the coherence property holds for all hypersurface singularities, and we provide evidence and counter-examples as well as some interesting properties of the non-coherent fibers. To further study these processes, we conduct high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic simulations that include an embedded particle-in-cell model, allowing us to quantify how electromagnetic energy converts into kinetic energy during island merging. By employing an adaptive model, we can simulate reconnections at smaller scales, equivalent to several thousand Thomson lengths, and obtain detailed information about the electron distribution. Our findings reveal that as the adaptivity level decreases, the electromagnetic energy conversion rate and kinetic energy production rate increase, but eventually level off. Furthermore, we observe that the most efficient kinetic energy production occurs at lower stopping criteria, and that our results are consistent with previous studies. Our simulation data also enable us to analyze the energetic electron population and provide a quantitative assessment of the island's dynamics during the entire merging process. Additionally, we can compare our magnetohydrodynamic results with those from full magnetohydrodynamic simulations, demonstrating good agreement and validating the use of embedded particle-in-cell models to investigate reconnection and island merging. Our work contributes valuable insights to the study of magnetic reconnection and island merging, and paves the way for the application of these models in simulating various astrophysical and space plasma phenomena. Given the high computational efficiency of these models, they can be utilized to simulate reconnections at much larger scales, such as those encountered in solar flares, neutron star mergers, and other catastrophic events. Our models also hold potential for the simulation of various laboratory and space plasma experiments. We propose Scribe, a novel approach in Software Engineering that mimics the
concept of the SCRIBE, a prominent social club in the HBO series, through a
algorithmic social simulation of dominant and submissive dynamics between
programmers and their trainees. Scribe's objective is to determine if a
subordinate's code revisions enhance the dominant's program or simply act as
complimentary work. This can be achieved by assessing how the combined efforts
of the subordinate and dominant contribute to the overall success of the
programmatic endeavor. Our research seeks to identify the specific characteristics that a subordinate developer should exhibit in order to be an effective and valuable addition to a dominant engineer's programmatic endeavors. Through our findings, we aim to provide a framework for a new algorithmic method that can be utilized for various software development purposes. Additionally, we hope to gain insight into how the proposed social simulation can be applied to real-world programmer interactions. To date, our research has yielded two actionable outcomes - one regarding the optimal traits of a subordinate developer and another providing guidance on the ideal characteristics of a dominant developer. Moving forward, we intend to delve deeper into the properties of the code revisions produced by the subordinate and dominant developers, as well as the temporal dynamics of their interactions. Furthermore, we aim to conduct a study involving human participants to validate our theoretical model and make a more informed assessment of the proposed social simulation. Ultimately, we hope to develop a more comprehensive understanding of programmer interactions, as well as the underlying principles of the social simulation. To support our research, we have made the source code for our social simulation publicly available. Additionally, we have created a webpage that showcases our results and provides a clear explanation of our algorithmic method.
